The Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies.
Volume Number 21.
The *Śrīmahānayaprakāśa*,
composed by the venerable and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Śrī Śitikaṇṭhācārya;
[dedicated to] the Great King of Kaśmīra, the Sun of the Dharma of Śrī Bhārata.
At the Pratividyāprakāśa (Research) Institute established by the illustrious Pratāpasiṃha-vara,
by its director, the Mahāmahopādhyāya Paṇḍita Mukundarāma Śāstrin.
Having collected [the materials] with the assistance of other scholars at the designated office, and after processing them through editing, pagination, annotation, and so forth,
[it was presented] in a modern, accessible, and refined style approved by Western scholarly circles.
Having been refined through editorial revisions,
it was printed at the Tattvavivecaka Press in Mumbai and brought into publication.
Saṃvat 1975; Christian year 1918.
Śrīnagara, Kashmir. (All rights regarding the publication, printing, and other matters of this book [are reserved].)
[They] have been brought under control by the most excellent of the great kings who have spoken [thus].
Salutations to Śiva, whose body is the glorious Great Light.
Now...
The Mahānayaprakāśa,
composed by the venerable Mahāmāheśvara Ācārya Rājānaka Śitikaṇṭha Ācārya,
and commented upon by that very same teacher.
May that divine, peaceful ground of confidence, which illumines the ten regions,
and from which the flood of consciousness arises as the word "Śiva-Brahman," shine for the virtuous.
She who, having made the six paths of the four eggs her own stomach, swoons [in ecstasy], and for whom phenomenal expansion and liberation are equal—may that slender-waisted Kula protect us. (2)
May the power Raudrī be victorious, she who, with her firmly established nature, employs various pleasing means to unite the dense multitude of the manifest universe within the heart of Maheśa. (3)
In this seat of Uḍḍiyāna, there is the supreme, most excellent knowledge and fierce conduct; likewise, in the pair of seats to the east and west, named Akula and Kulamahā,
it is mixed with Śakti.

The splendor of these seats does not intermingle with one another in this way; rather, let this eternally great object, possessing a blazing luster, prevail through its sovereign majesty over the spreading light of the seats—[in the Kha manuscript, the reading is "through the sovereign majesty of the splendors"]. May it be victorious! || 4 ||
Having ascertained the path of mantras consisting of enumerated phonemes and words, I shall here explain the entire essence of what is expressed by them; let this be reflected upon. (5)
Now begins the composition.

May that [revelation] which was perceived from the great torrent of the Divine Current (divyaugha)—the thundering resonance of sound and meaning belonging to the Primordial Goddess—be for our benefit;
it is the source of the subtle waves of my own [experience] and has as its fruit the repose within one’s true nature. (1)

The construction of the words is as follows: "May that resonance of sound and meaning—which was perceived immediately after the great stream preceded by the Divine Current (divyaugha) has issued forth from the presence of the Primordial Goddess (Ādidevī), and which is the source of the subtle ripples of the Māyic [current]—be for us the fruit of resting in our own true nature (svarūpa). The intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*), however, is this: the Supreme Self—

From the divine current (*divyaugha*) whose nature is supreme speech (*parāvāc*) presided over by the goddesses such as Svarūpā, from the great flow in the form of *paśyantī*—whose essence is the vibration of the emerging resonance (*nādaspanda*)—there arises the expansion of *madhyamā* speech, which is inseparable from the signified and the signifier, and which is colored by the objects being conceptualized. (p. 4)

The "thundering of word and meaning" (*śabdārthavisphūrjathuḥ*): both word (*śabda*) and meaning (*artha*), that is, name and form (*nāmarūpa*), the signifier and the signified; their "thundering" (*visphūrjathuḥ*) is their manifestation. This very [manifestation], being of the nature of *vaikharī* speech and conjoined with its signified objects, takes the form of the shimmering waves of *māyā*, and is synonymous with the phenomenal world (*viśvaprapañca*). It is the primary cause (*nidāna*) of that [world].

The locus of origination, characterized as being uncharacterized—that manifestation of speech culminating in *vaikharī*, which unfolds through its respective denotata and is presided over by *parāvāk*—is thus the manifestation of the fourfold speech, culminating in *vaikharī* and presided over by *parāvāk*. (Note:
In manuscript *ka*, the reading is "the *vaikharī* of the fourfold speech.")

The one who is conscious is the very nature of consciousness; likewise, the mass of objects to be expressed—which is the domain of the threefold speech and is being conceptualized—consists of the nature of both existence and non-existence. In both ways, this entire cosmic manifestation is merely the expansion of consciousness; it has consciousness as its cause, is established in consciousness, consists of consciousness, and rests solely in pure consciousness.

"May the fruit of resting in one's own true nature belong to us"—meaning, may it always and for everyone culminate in the experience of the great purpose (*mahārtha*) whose form is thus pervasive; this is indicated by the verse of salutation.

(5) Having thus contemplated the true nature of the Supreme Goddess, he speaks in order to pay homage to the Goddess Makāra, who is the form of the Guru: "She reveals her own body as both void and non-void, as the supreme and the subordinate."
May he who is like a variegated creeper engraved with auspicious signs of prosperity be victorious! || 2 ||
The body of the Goddess is her own true nature, which is both supreme and non-supreme, pure and yet the form of phenomenal manifestation;

it is both empty and non-empty—the "empty" being the nature of pure consciousness and not a state of mere non-existence, while the "non-empty" is that which is sullied by *māyā*. In both ways, it is the manifold variety of the Goddess's very own nature.

"May the illustrious Goddess Makaradevi, who manifests various forms in the shape of engraved leaves and is the form of the Primordial Guru, be victorious"— with this divine verse, the praise of the Blessed Lady is performed; for although the entire phenomenal universe is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Consciousness, it is nevertheless [worshipped] in the form of the well-awakened Śrī Maṅgalā.
"The primordial deity itself has been revealed"—thus the praise has been briefly indicated. || 2 ||
(p. 6) Then, in order to compose a hymn suited to his own inclination using a vernacular accessible to all, he says:

"O Goddess! What kind of person in this world is a devourer? A terrifying one who would eat [all]. One who possesses infinite power, a consumer of men, who would cut away their very intentions. [Ka0 Pu0: āśaya]
The reading is "bhakṣeta" (he should eat). || 3 ||
"The Goddess who is intent on devouring the world..."—according to the course of the scriptures, the one Supreme Goddess alone shines forth in her entirety;
she radiates, having cast aside the adversary known as duality. Having done what? To this he says: "devouring the world."
Time creates all beings, making the world laugh; Time destroys all creatures.
Time remains awake while others sleep; indeed, Time is insurmountable.
By saying this, having devoured Bhairava— who is by nature the devourer of the world—

Time, assuming the form of Bhairava, creates everything from the cause of the universe down to the smallest insect [in the Ka-pu manuscript, the reading is "from Bhairava down to the smallest insect"].
By the power of whose desire— [the rest of the verse follows] — ||
Because it has been said thus, Time is Bhairava; and he is of the nature of Sound (*nāda*), whose form is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). As it has been stated:
"Everything, both the stationary and the moving, is the food of the vital breath."

Thus, having devoured and dissolved that vital breath which was acting like Bhairava, and having reached the ground of the breathless, which is the culmination of sound (*nāda*)—as the reading in the Ka manuscript is *nidānam āsādya*—what kind of state is this? To this he says: "Endless" (*ananta*), meaning endless because the nine waves are infinite, and thus they take the form of waves.
The powers began to devour them, as the scripture says:
"The goddesses arising from the pores of the skin, blazing with the light that illuminates the world—
having vomited forth the universe, those dark ones, having swallowed the universe, constitute a single mouthful."

Thus, because there is no movement either within the body or externally, the expansion of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) has subsided; she is free from limiting adjuncts (*anupādhi*) and undivided. Likewise, "nīrāji" means in her own nature which is stainless (*nīrājika*), pure, and unmixed with the turbidity of duality; or else, it refers to the Goddess.

At the great festival of his own empire, which consists of uninterrupted radiance, at a particular time for world conquest upon an exalted stage; nevertheless, even in a time when sovereignty has vanished, the kingdom is lost,
all order is stolen away by the exhaustion of mental constructs, and there is no restraint— [she], possessing tranquility, becomes calm.

"Leaving behind the waves" means remaining established in her own true nature (*svarūpa*). By thinning out the support—that is, the substratum—she manifests a waveless essence and shines with a peaceful form;
this is the threefold meaning. Furthermore, she pacifies the "intention," which is the mind (*citta*), through "carving," that is, by means of purification.
Making herself free from desire by calming the flow of longing, she shines forth.
Having thus praised the form of the Goddess—customary, pleasing, and peaceful—he spoke these rising words:
"O Akula, you who touch and pervade; O Bodhāraṇa, you who have entered Kula; O Ahalī, you who possess the power of the Guru.
You are the knot, the wheel, the support, and the upholder; she who is of manifold forms has been victorious. (4)

Touching the form that transcends the *akula* and the *kula*, she is all-pervasive and the fire-drill (*araṇi*) for awakening—the place of origin of awakening—and thus she has entered the *kula*. She is the power (*śakti*) whose form is "ahala"—a compound formed by the elision of the middle term (*madhyapadalopa*), where *aha* means "not" and *la* means "plough" (*hala*).
Thus, she is "devoid of the form of a plough," meaning she is devoid of the shape of a distinct line in the form of a plough.

The power (śakti) has the form of the letter *ha* and is without consonants (*ahala*). Alternatively, she is called *ahalā* because she takes (*lāti*), that is, grasps and pervades, the letters *a* and *ha*, which are the first and last letters, in the form of the utterance of the Mātṛkā [in the Ka-pu manuscript, the reading is "in the form of the movement of the Mātṛkā"]. Alternatively, she is *ahalā* because she has no consonants (*hal*)—she is the Kuṇḍalinī in the form of vowels, not yet having attained the script.
Being uttered, it should resound and arise like *guñjā* seeds, tearing asunder the knots (*granthi*), the wheels (*cakra*), and the supports (*ādhāra*). From the location of the *ahala*, this power,
which is the nature of the *udāna* energy, acts as the tearer of the knots, the wheels, and the supports during its state of emergence.

May she who provides the opening for upward movement manifest through the manifestation of sound; thus, may she who possesses such manifold forms be ever victorious. And so it is said in the *Āmāvāsyātriṃśikā*:
"He who is that Śiva, both supreme and non-supreme, peaceful, all-pervading, and great."
For he is immeasurable, infinite, all-pervading, and the Lord of all lords.
She possesses an innate power that consists of all powers and is supreme;
as the nature of will, knowledge, and action, she alone exists in manifold ways.

Having internally gathered those various manifestations of that [Energy] which have emerged in manifested form through their effects, she abides in the state of Śiva, the equilibrium of aesthetic flavor.
Thus, because she is the power whose purpose is vision,
the Goddess has a gross body as the universe (*viśvatanu*), while being subtle in the form of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
She is the supreme (*parā*), eternally risen, peaceful, and her essential nature is the reality of Brahman (*brahmasattā*).

As stated in the scripture: first, one should contemplate the goddess of the limit (*paryantadevī*); then the Supreme (*parā*) as "the pervasive maintenance of consciousness" (*vyāpakabodhāraṇa*), which is the *akulachutta*;

then the Intermediate-Parā (*parāparā*) in her subtle form as "the maintenance of the support" (*ādhāravidhāraṇa*), which is the *kulagata-ahalīśattagumūna*, the *ganthicakra*; and likewise the Inferior (*aparā*) in her gross form as "of manifold forms" (*anekarūpa*). Thus.

Praised in three ways, and though she is threefold, she is one alone; thus, by virtue of her oneness of self (*ātmaikātmya*), may she be victorious as her own essential nature (*svasvarūpa*). Pervading the ground of the *Akula*, she is the mother who gives birth to the sparks of consciousness—those whose manifestations are fixed according to their respective cognitions. Thus, though she possesses manifold forms, may she, being one alone, be victorious, through the rejection of all opposing views.

"May she, whose nature is an unobstructed and undivided manifestation, expand through an empire under a single umbrella"—thus, at the beginning of this treatise, it is *Śakti* herself, who is the primary subject, that must first be saluted.
In a salutation, there is the subordination of the worshipper and the exaltation of the object of praise; for as [the former] has a very limited scope, while [the latter] has a vast scope.
By the statement of Vijaya, "it becomes included within [the preceding]," it is understood that the very purpose is prostration; therefore, such a description was made. || 4 ||

Having thus praised the threefold form in this way, he speaks in order to grasp the fundamental Śāmbhava form: "The limit of the limits, that which encompasses all, the cause of the differentiation of speech, both with cause and without cause."
The wheel of the sky-farer has flashed forth; that great-souled one, Akka, conquers and remains without abode. || 5 ||

The meaning of the sentence is that he alone, the one of great purpose, triumphs. That Self, whose stretching out of the foot extends as far as the expansion of the wheel of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) through the sense of "I-ness" (*ahantā*), is the one in whom the state of great purpose has been established; he is truly one because, by the aforementioned process, the womb of the power of the expansion of duality has been torn asunder.
Likewise, may he who is the crowning ornament of the sixty-fifth position—the conclusion of the sixty-fourth stage to be described hereafter—be victorious upon the ground of creation and dissolution.
And at the completion of the meaning of the sentence, his specific qualification is stated in brief: "without abode" (*aniketu*).
Because it pervades all directions, locations, times, births, and individual entities— which serve as delimiters through their respective restrictions—
with its own single essential nature, [the Lord] extends His feet everywhere in unity;
thus He is "without abode" (*aniketa*), as the Rājānaka, the author of the *Pratyabhijñā*, has praised Him.
Whatever may be an obscuration of Being for living beings,
that very thing is not at all an obscuration of Being for devotees.
Thus it is said. And a certain wise man has declared:
"Whatever is imagined as an obscuration, by that very thing, alas, this body blazes forth intensely;
let it be the nature of Bhairava, which is in reality the manifestation of the principle of non-duality."

Thus; by the word "that" (*sa*), he implies three further statements: that which is the limit, the boundary, the place of establishment, of even that "other" who is the ultimate beyond the final [levels] and who dwells upon the second stage—as the author of the *Pratyabhijñā* has said.
Salutations to the ocean of Śiva-consciousness, whose form is the undivided resting place for all the various streams of cognition, and who possesses the body of the subject.

(13) Thus: regarding the existence or non-existence of the objects of words, the final limit in the determination of each respective action—such as "this is blue" or "this is yellow"—is the determinative cognition that "this is thus. As it has been sung:
"O Pārtha, every action in its entirety culminates in knowledge."
Thus it is said; likewise:
"Indeed, there is nothing in this world as purifying as knowledge.
And so forth.
"Having attained knowledge, one reaches supreme peace without delay.

This [knowledge] is dependent upon the senses; and because of their diversity, there is multiplicity for those [senses] when they are defiled by objects. The supreme locus of establishment is the pure Self, whose nature is the Supreme Word (*parāvāk*); and of those Selves as well—

The state of culmination (*niṣṭhāsthāna*) is the limit—the place of rest, the Supreme Self, the Great Purpose (*mahārtha*). As it is said in the *Saṃvāda*: "That which is both supreme and non-supreme, the peaceful Śiva, all-pervading and great."
For he is immeasurable, infinite, all-pervading, and the Great Lord (Maheśvara). [In the Ka manuscript, the reading is "the Lord of Lords who is all-pervading."]

Thus, he alone is the one named "the Great Purpose" (*mahārtha*). This very [reality] is, for the dualists, characterized as Man, Power, and Śiva; yet it is further distinguished by the terminology of Self, Knowledge, and Śiva, or by being the Knower, the Knowledge, and the Supreme Self.
It is that wherein the stages of knowledge (*jñāna-bhūmikā*) consist of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, and its nature is knowledge itself.

In the stage of Turya at the end of that, the Self exists in the form of the knower; in the stage beyond Turya (Turyātīta), which transcends that, it is the Supreme Self—this is the great meaning. Likewise, while residing in the physical body composed of elements, it maintains the state of "I am the embodied one" (dehin);
thus it is "Piṇḍastha" (established in the body), because— [Note: According to the Kaśmīra manuscript, the reading is "sthitiṃ badhnāti" (binds the state).]

Bound within the *piṇḍa*, residing in the first *puryaṣṭaka*, clothed in the sheath of the body, and enveloped by the functions of the intellect, the senses, and the organs of action—the *karmātman* is called "residing in the *piṇḍa*" (*piṇḍastha*). For him, the power of *nāda* is the primary cause; as for the state of "residing in the word" (*padastha*), it consists of the form of waves.
The *mātṛkā* is primordial nature (*prakṛti*), whose form is the power of sound (*śabdaśakti*), the expansion of the manifold of denoters;
it is the manifestation (*vivarta*) of phonemes, words, mantras, and names; it has the form of the "central city" (*puryaṣṭaka*);
though appearing as both internal and external, it is the form of the pervasive subject (*pramātṛ*) who pervades both within and without, and its specific differentiation is as follows.
Through the unification of *nāda* and *bindu*, impelled by fire and wind [the reading in the Kha manuscript is "impelled by wind alone"],

it inflates the *kanda* [the reading in the Ka manuscript is "inflated by karma"]; being of the nature of light (*taijasa*), it becomes the object of the sense of form, containing within it the paths of *kalā*, *tattva*, and *bhuvana*, and becoming the essence of the *bindu* principle.

The expansion of the power (*śakti*) blazing forth from the uttered [mantra] is established in form; it is the third *puryaṣṭaka* (eightfold city), because the elements, subtle elements, and vital breaths, joined with the instruments and the powers of the qualities,
constitute the *puryaṣṭaka*, as well as the knots, the senses, the fingers, and so forth, along with the intellect of the twelve.

Thus, although there are three modes, they are here in fact one; transcending that, it is the form-transcending (rūpātīta), consisting of the state of the fourth (turya), pure, and of the nature of the Self, which is the perfect self-reflection. Transcending even that, this is the Great Meaning (mahārtha) which transcends everything. Furthermore, it is that which belongs to the traditions (āmnāyas) existing at the ultimate limit.

The supreme *uttarāmnāya* is even more excellent than that; it is the tradition of the nine wheels (*navacakrasampradāya*), which stands at the very end of the sequence beginning from the thirty-six divisions. This is the "Great Meaning" (*mahārtha*). Likewise, both the earth and water, mentioned first and clearly manifest as the great elements (*mahābhūta*), [are present] in the third element called fire.

As they proceed toward dissolution, even that third element called fire subsides into the fourth element called air; and that fourth element called air, whose nature is vibration, attains a state of equilibrium within the fifth element, the ether of the elements, which is motionless— thus, the ether of the elements [is the ground] of the universe.

The limit of that which consists of the great elements is the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*), and that [elemental space] finds its foundation in the supreme space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*). Thus, the supreme space of consciousness is the limit of that [elemental space]; furthermore, the ultimate space (*parākāśa*) is the limit of even that. As the scripture says:
Ever-arisen in the external space, the space of consciousness, and the supreme space,
a certain unprecedented Great Being, the Sun, shines everywhere.

Thus, may the Supreme Space (*parākāśa*), which dwells upon the third stage, be the Great Purpose (*mahārtha*); likewise, it is the cause of the differentiation of phonemes (*varṇavibhāga*). Because there is an absence of agency preceded by gross volition—such as "having done this, I shall do that"—it is the cause (*kāraṇa*) and the motive (*hetu*), and that [cause] is by means of the Supreme (*pareṇa*).

Because it has not been produced by anyone, the Self-Sovereign is without cause; He is the cause of the manifestation (*vivarta*) of names consisting of phonemes— from the letter *a* to *ha* as contained in the *mātṛkā*, as well as the distinction and differentiation of the social classes (*varṇa*), such as Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.

The cause that fashions the diversity therein is what is called the mutual difference and distinction [of things] by virtue of their exclusion from both similar and dissimilar entities; however, it does not act with a gross intention like a potter. Regarding this, the true nature of the commentary has been explained repeatedly; thus, [the wheel of the sky-faring goddesses]... [end of fragment].

That Self is He in whom the wheel of transmigratory existence vibrates— established therein and shining forth by His own pervasive majesty through the expansion of His own power, which, by means of the gateway of the "greatness" of the circle of rays, possesses the state of greatness extending to the limits of all objects, and which is completely filled with an immersion reaching those very limits; it is like the wheel of stars.

Although existing in various individuals and appearing in manifold ways, it is in reality one; when it perceives its own self as existing in various individuals— just as mercury (rasendra) spreads in many forms— and conducts itself through an undivided manifestation as a unity, then it should be understood as the *paramātman* (the Supreme Self), and that too is so.
He is to be venerated as the one of great significance; he is the sixteenth... And likewise, in the Brāhmaṇa of the Yajurveda, his state as the seventeenth is taught:
"He becomes the all-encompassing seventeenth; he is the seventeenth."
"Prajāpati attains Prajāpati himself.
Thus it is stated in the Brāhmaṇa of the Sāmaveda:
"Everything becomes seventeenfold."
Thus, he is the seventeenth embodied soul (*dehī*), who stands as the supreme limit beyond the fifteen— the elements, the organs of action, and the doors of the organs of cognition—

and who, being outward-turned, is of the nature of karma; likewise, sound is the quality of space (*viyat*), sound and touch are the qualities of air (*vāyu*), and [the following] are the qualities of fire (*tejas*).
Those called sound, touch, and form; the qualities of water—sound, touch, form, and taste;

and the qualities of earth—sound, touch, form, taste, and smell: thus there are fifteen. The intellect (*buddhi*) is the sixteenth. The inner self (*antarātman*), bound by those qualities, is the seventeenth. Likewise...
The ten rays presiding over the doors of the intellect, the organs of action, and the senses;

the five powers of consciousness, bliss, will, knowledge, and action—these constitute fifteen. The sixteenth is the pure, awakened power (*śakti*). That very self (*ātman*), consisting of the full egoity (*pūrṇāhaṃkṛt*), transcends them.
The seventeenth is the Supreme Self—this is the great significance; He alone is conventionally designated as the "Ninefold Self" (navātman).
And so, in the Śruti, in the sequence of laying the bricks with the Sāvitra, Nāciketa, and Cāturhotrika mantras, [He is described] in the lower layer (adhaściti)—

And with the middle layers and the highest layers, the ninth self, situated in the midst of those eight— the head, the two shoulders, the two wings, the two hips, and the tail— of that altar-structure, is to be laid down.
Likewise,
earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind,
intellect, and ego— thus is this nature of mine divided eightfold.
"Another [form] is this... and so on, as in the meaning of the *Gītā*. (p.
19) Earth, fire, the sacrificer, the sun, water, wind, and the moon;
And space—these are the forms... ||

Thus, the ninth Self situated within the midst of the eightfold group of primordial nature (*prakṛty-aṣṭaka*) is the presiding lord of the first *puryaṣṭaka*, which consists of the bodily sheath; and this ninth Self is also sevenfold,
belonging to the sixth Self which is bound by the five rays of the vital breath (*vāha*).
The seventh resting place is the Supreme Self (paramātman), as the scripture states:
"Thus the pervasion is twelvefold and established as sevenfold. This is according to the perspective of the Seven Lords of the Body (saptanāthapiṇḍa); likewise:

"Twelve-fold in nature, abiding in twelve... Thus, he is the presiding lord of the twelve stations of the rays (*marīci*), extending his feet through the ego-sense (*ahantā*) within the twelve flows; and in reality, he is the thirteenth self, situated at the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*).
Within that too, at the end of the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta), is the Supreme Self (paramātman); the meaning is that He is its illuminator and is entered into it.

When it is said that "the one [Self] is the illuminator within the end of the twelve," this is praised in the Vārttika: "The Self shines as if playing through delusion before the senses, perceived in its entirety."
I praise that Supreme Self, my own, whose glory is unfading.

Thus, this very Mahārtha—consisting of the six, the eight, the twelve, the thirteen, the sixteen, and the sixty-four—is praised as residing at the ultimate limit. Now, what indeed is the "great object" (*mahān arthaḥ*) that is denoted by the term Mahārtha? To this it is said: in this [system] where all is reduced to the One... [the remainder of the universe].
Whatever extraordinary qualities exist in the state of the seed, all of them arise within that one [reality] alone;

for what else could be the vessel for the term "Great Purpose" (*mahārtha*) than the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*), which is free from limiting conditions and characterized by indivisible manifestation? Thus, this is the indication of the various aspects: self-quiescence and immersion into one's own essential nature.
In the discourse on worship—those things denoted by the term "Mahārtha" are five... O! [They are:
the peace of one's own nature, the pure consciousness during emergence, and the universal majesty.
Arising solely from external conditions... the body of the Goddess is twofold, consisting entirely of the manifold expansion of worldly existence.

The form of emergence (*vyutthāna-rūpa*) is experienced as if it were being conventionally designated; thus, this twofold form of emergence is a state of constant absorption (*nitya-samādhāna*). In this way, there is a threefold immersion (*tridhā-veśa*) through the division of Śambhu, Śakti, and Aṇḍa; and manifestation (*prathā*) consists of both the initial face and the subsequent discourse.

The definitive [instruction] regarding the two—possession (*āveśa*) and worship (*pūjā*)—is set forth in the form of verbal expression: "The sequence of worship, by its very nature, is permeated by the form of discourse and possession;
it is the cause for attaining one's true nature through the practice of the lineage."
Likewise,
[the worship] separated from the limbs of worship prescribed by the traditional succession is devoid of the proper procedure and serves merely as the utilization of material substances.
Or, a householder may subsist on the nectar of social gatherings with those of equal aspirations;
for his practice of eating boiled rice alone serves merely to satisfy his natural desires.
Out of the sixfold state of reality, which one is appropriate to be designated as "Mahārtha"?
Is this single name "Mahārtha" applied to these six when they are combined—
meaning that the six combined together are called one "Mahārtha"— or rather, do these six individually and separately constitute this [Mahārtha]?

In response to the doubt—“Is this Great Purpose (mahārtha) also called ‘Great Purpose’ because it is designated separately by the term ‘Great Purpose’?”—it is resolved as follows: In both ways, the designation of the Great Purpose is capable of being expressed;
that which expresses its own essential nature proceeds through the primary mode of the expression of the Great Purpose.
Since that [result] is attained through a lineage of succession, this [teaching] is the basis for it elsewhere.
Thus it is said. In this context, "perfectly tranquil" (*suśāntā*) refers to that which is real, denoted by the term "the Great Purpose" (*mahārthapada*).
This very immersion into one's own true nature (*svasvarūpāveśa*) is the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*), a point of non-dispute for all.
And for the sake of attaining rest in that [nature], there is the abode of the Goddess (*devīdhāma*), which is experienced as having the form of the entire universe.

May it become the cause for attaining one's true nature (*svarūpa*). Furthermore, *āveśa* (possession) consists of three types: the first is the *āṇava* [āveśa], which consists of the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*);

the second is the *śākta*, which is devoid of the agitation of the vital breath and is accompanied by bliss (*sānanda*); and the third is the *śāmbhava*, which transcends the experience of bliss and is the closest to resting in one's own essential nature (*svasvarūpaviśrānti*).

Let it be designated as "Mahārtha" (the Great Purpose) because it is intent upon attaining the nature already described; and let its exposition— from mouth to mouth— be that which, independent of everything else, determines the immersion (*āveśa*) into worship, clearly revealing one's own true nature like a mango fruit held in the hand, and thus figuratively designated by the name Mahārtha.

Let it be so; even the sequence of worship, though by its very nature included within both [the means and the goal] for the purpose of describing the descent [of power], and though non-different from one's own true nature when considered according to the actual state of things, becomes— when presented as a process—
the cause for attaining the ultimate stage through the lineage, by virtue of being a means of attainment through metaphorical designation.

Let it be designated by the name "Great Purpose" (*mahārtha*). How can this so-called "conduct" (*caryā*)—which consists merely of eating and drinking, is devoid of any prescribed duty (*itikartavyatā*), and is a sixth [category] distinct from the [five perfections]—be spoken of?
Is it for the sake of fulfilling one's desires or attaining pleasure, or is it for the sake of fulfilling the meaning of one's own scripture (*svāgama*)?
Among these three positions, that which is called the fulfillment of the meaning of one's own scripture—

which constitutes the primary element— cannot possibly be devoid of worship, whether it be undertaken with a desire for material goods as part of the ritual preparations, or out of worldly conformity.
The mere partial recollection of the sequence, when being put into practice, does not accord with propriety;
and the attainment of happiness, though obtainable through many means, does not achieve established status under the designation of "worship" (pūjā);
furthermore, as for the fulfillment of desire, is it independent or dependent upon the rule (samaya)? In that regard—
The well-established traditions (*susamayāḥ*) cannot be divided because they constitute the constituent parts of the sequence of worship;

furthermore, the independent and unstable impulse of the will (*icchāveśa*) of the subjects (*pramātṛ*), being filled to infinity, is indeed difficult to satisfy and thus ineffective. And in some cases, this [will] serves for the transformation of a substance.
As the great sages such as Ātreya and others have said: "How could meat from marshy or arid lands, even when prepared according to the prescribed rules,
be properly digested without the accompaniment of liquor?"

Thus it has been taught by way of its role in digesting what has been eaten and drunk. Likewise: "That is no gathering which is bereft of wine; that is no assembly which is abandoned by wine; there is no amorous play without wine, and no appetizer bereft of wine."

Thus, how can that which is conceived as an accessory to enjoyment— being offered as a *bali* in the form of deities such as the lords of the eight wheels (*aṣṭacakreśvara*) and being manifested as an instrument for the primary worship— be placed among the common utensils, and how can it be introduced into the midst of the consumption of leftovers?
A large vessel of liquor fosters great impropriety, whereas [the vessel] that purifies the remnants does not; thus,
by turning the primary implement of worship into a means for sensual enjoyment,
what terrible fruit born from the violation of the *samaya* will one not incur?
One who is devoted to liquor, meat, the enjoyment of the topknot, and attachment to women;
who is fickle, intent on the linga, and base—is not a vessel for the Great Purpose.

Thus, the position that [the Mahārtha] is merely a semblance of solitary practice has been refuted. In this way, it is established that there are exactly five objects of the designation "Mahārtha" as denoters—either directly or through a lineage—namely: the means for the undivided reality, the means for its parts, and other means which are the causes for the accomplishment of those means. Thus.
This has been stated in connection with the present topic; this is the procedure for prostration.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Mahānayaprakāśa composed by the venerable teacher Śitikaṇṭhācārya. || 1 ||
The Illumination of the Great Way (Mahānayaprakāśa)
Now begins the second chapter. (p. 25) Now follows the sequence for introducing the text; therein, first, is the sequence for introducing the creation.
The first resonance (nirghoṣa) of the Supreme Śiva, who is beyond the other, is the expansion of Śakti;
the pair that arises as the splendor of Sadāśiva is the expansion of Nāda, the seed of the universe. || 1 ||

Thus, that which is the couple— the eternal, innate nature consisting of the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*)— of that supreme Śiva and that supreme Śakti, which is the indestructible form of the Supreme Lord; from that, there is the first, primordial *spanda* (vibration).
The sprouting forth [of the universe] is like a sudden thunderclap in a stainless, windless sky;
it is the natural emergence of the *nāda*—the seed of the universe and the essence of Sadāśiva—which has arisen from the Couple.
This is the state of manifestation in the form of its arising. Thus ends the supreme creation. || 1 ||

And in that union consisting of Agni and Soma, the sound (nāda) and the drop (bindu) meet; the Lord’s form is the Word, its meaning is the people, and here the agent of consciousness is the assembly of wills. 2.

Through the conjunction and merging of Agni and Soma, the Bindu necessarily follows as being attached to Nāda, who is Sadāśiva; like the meaning to a word, Īśvara is inseparable and the very life-force [of the manifestation]. Therefore, from this Īśvara, whose form consists of the Bindu presided over by Nāda, this [universe] proceeds with a conscious agent.

The universal expansion is preceded by will; inseparable from that Lord Sadāśiva, whose nature is sound (*nāda*) and whose sole body is light, is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is the Lord (*īśvara*) and the Point (*bindu*).

It is the secondary designation (*upākhyā*) of the primary manifestation (*prakhyā*); it is like bliss to pure consciousness, like the downward breath (*apāna*) to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), or like [the power] to the Person (*puruṣa*).

The primary principle (*pradhāna*) is such that, just as in the world the object follows the word, so too in the creation of the universe Soma is conjoined with Fire (*agni*). Likewise, this "drop" (*bindu*) of sound, through its state of union, is the cause of the vibration of the universe; thus, when one relies upon this nature of Fire and Soma, there occurs an intentional act produced by a conscious agent.

The creation is governed by the Lord; here, moreover, desire alone is the material cause, and not—as in the case of the Brahma-creation—the production from the gross elements. Furthermore, this is not like the system of the Theistic Cārvākas, wherein the manifestation of the universe occurs within space and its dissolution likewise occurs in space. Thus ends the section on the divine creation. || 2 ||
And to manifest that very [point], he says:
"The face is the mirror; know the fivefold speech as its reflection.
The supreme ether is the will, consciousness, and the object of desire; this is the awakening to the elemental ether. (3)

The whiteness residing in the face reflected on the surface of a mirror, as well as the utterance of speech, and likewise the fivefold cognition produced by the five senses— this entire specialized knowledge does not appear as having been transferred by way of reflection; and thus it is this [reality].

The elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), even though it is a reflection of the ether of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), is indeed insentient and devoid of awakening; for the sequence of will and consciousness has dissolved into the supreme ether (*paranabhas*). The expansion of will exists only in the ether of consciousness and not in the insentient elemental ether, even though the latter is pure, infinite, and all-pervasive like the ether of consciousness—as it has been said:
Having cast the mind into the external space— which is the eternal, supportless, void, all-pervasive, and free from mental constructs— one should enter the supreme space.

Thus, there is the conventional usage of the term "supreme space" (*parākāśa*) by way of its similarity to external space; nevertheless, not all properties of the example can be applied to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*),
for it is intended that only those common properties (*sādhāraṇadharma*) are to be transferred (*saṃcārin*), as constrained by the specific intention [of the speaker].

The conventional usage consists of the analogy and the subject of the analogy; for this reason—from which cause—this "elemental space" (*bhūtavyoma*) is unawakened, devoid of cognition, and inert by nature. In this way: just as a face, though distinguished by all its features, is reflected in a mirror, yet its heaviness—that is, its weight—is not perceived by a scale.
Likewise, the cleverness of verbal proliferation and the proficiency of the cognitive faculties do not reflect in a mirror;
similarly, the attributes of the supreme ether and the attributes of the ether of consciousness cannot be conceived within the elemental ether. || 3 ||
(p. 29) Now he describes that process of the creation of Īśvara:
"His [Īśvara's] manifestation of will (*icchā*) is fourfold—consisting of Raudrī, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Ambā;
after will comes knowledge (*jñāna*), which is partless (*niṣkala*), and from it descend the Great Elements (*mahābhūta*). (4)
That from which there is the expansion of will is the "expansion of will" (*icchāprasara*); the Lord is the cause of that expansion of will.

The letter *A* consists of four parts (*catuṣkala*), whose parts (*kalā*) are Raudrī, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Ambā. Arising from that is the emergence of will (*icchāsamudaya*), which exists at the very forefront of knowledge (*jñānaprākkoṭibhāvī*). Thus...
Knowledge, which is partless and preceded by will, is the instrument for the creation of the universe;
from that alone the great elements descend.
Thus, the expansion arises from the void, and from that expansion this world has emerged.
From the letter *a* the universe has arisen; the universe is the world consisting of five elements.

Thus, according to the perspective of the scriptures, the letter *a* has manifested first; likewise, in the transformation of name (*nāmavivarta*), it is the initial phoneme produced at the commencement of the *mātṛkā*, and in the transformation of form (*rūpavivarta*), it is the nature of the abyss (*avaṭarūpa*)—[in the Kha manuscript, the reading is *cābudharūpa*]. In both ways, it is indeed the letter *a*.
The primordial limit of the universal expansion is that very [consciousness]; because it is all-pervasive, it is the universe (*viśva*).

The formation of its limbs occurs through the four digits (*kalā*) of its form (*akāra*); and among those, at the beginning, Raudrī is the head of this [form] (the *kha* manuscript corrects this to "Raudrī is the head of the letter *a*").
The mouth is proclaimed as Vāmā;
Ambikā is said to be the arms, and Jyeṣṭhā is remembered as the weapon.

By such statements as these, this tradition of the first letter [of the alphabet] is according to the mouth of the Guru: thus, mere will alone is the instrument for the creation of the universe, and not the primordial matter of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) as held by those who maintain the reality of external objects;
likewise, will is the equipment of the Creator of the Universe, and the creation of the universe [proceeds from it]; and therefore, the great elements [are derived from that will].

At the very moment they are desired, these [objects] arise spontaneously; they are employed according to their utility, not by way of a process involving accumulated materials, like the creation of Brahmā, because this divine creation is without any external material cause (nirupādāna). || 4 ||
Now, he describes that creation of the elements which is presided over by the Brahma-creation:
Then, as at the beginning, from the void arose space; from that, the wind attached to its limb; from that, fire; from both of these, water; and from that, the earth, the support of all directions.
(P. 31) Both were without form; from fire and water came the earth, the support of the quarters. (5)
Then, from the cavity of the first letter, space arose; the wave of wind clung to its limb;
from the friction of both, fire was produced; and the solidified water of perspiration became the earth.

Then, from the cavity of the primordial letter within the heart, space (nabhas) manifested; clinging to its limbs was the internal wave of the wind (prābhañjanī ūrmi). From the friction—the mutual impact—of both that space and that wind, fire (pāvaka) arose; and from that pressing, water (āpas) emerged.

They flow like liquid sweat; and when vāta is predominant, due to the abundance of cold touch, they become solidified and manifest as the state of earth. Those very waters, within the womb, take the form of semen and blood, and being nourished in succession through the stages of the *ghanā*, *kalalā*, and *peśī*, they assume the state of the embryo (*garbha*). || 5 ||
He explains that very point in detail:
"The drops of blood and intoxication, O Jū, when split apart by the wind-obscurity, merge with that; those which were given to the body at night became the swellings of the cheeks. (6)

The two drops of blood and semen are distinct; the wave of *vāta* arises for their union, from which the tradition of the primordial syllable (*ādyakṣara*) emerges. Such a knotted knot, in the form of a phoneme (*varṇa*), has manifested, as the Siddhapādas have indicated.
Earth, water,
fire, air, and space— these five elements, having assumed their respective forms, enter into the body and manifest as its constituent parts.
Thus it is said. For here, the first part of the initial letter *ā* is the letter *ta*;

therein, the earth is situated below as the first numerical digit, the water is the central knot, the fire is the head in the shape of a *śṛṅgāṭaka*, and from there follows the portion situated at the back.

Due to its arrangement in the form of the letter *ra*, it is *repha*; because it is extended, it is characterized by space (*nabhas*) as that which covers. The transverse portion of the junction between those two letters, *ta* and *ra*, is the letter *ha* as air (*vāyu*).
Thus, this initial phoneme is bound together by these five [elements]; it is itself, in the creation of the elements, in the form of a pit (*āvaṭa*).
This is proclaimed through the vision of the Guru’s mouth; this very point is stated [in the scripture]: "Those who are established in the field of the Rāta. This is the time of birth. || 6 ||

In this regard, the expansion of each [organ] exists by virtue of its great significance; thus he says: Skin, flesh, teeth, nails, bone, marrow, blood, head, face, tongue, eyes, palate, stomach, anus, mouth, ears, heart, and nose. (7)
I am composed of the five elements and the five qualities; such is the manifestation of the realm of beings (*bhūtasarga*).
I have plunged into this whirlpool of worldly existence (*āvarta*), which is difficult to cross.
The Mānasapīṭha is extensive. || 8 ||

Skin, flesh, teeth, nails, and bones—this fivefold, solid element residing in the body is the earth-principle (*pṛthvītattva*). Lymph, blood, phlegm, fat, and marrow—this fivefold [element] is the water-principle (*jalatattva*). Anger, as well as the luster of the face—the fire residing in the mouth—and likewise the bodily heat, [constitute the fire-principle].

The fire of the eyes—the illuminating light residing in the eyes—and the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni); thus, the element of fire (tejas-tattva) is fivefold. Likewise, the vital breaths (prāṇas)—the five winds consisting of prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna—wherein prāṇa is preeminent, primary, and predominant.

It is called *prāṇa* because it breathes (*ana*) by distinguishing itself from other winds; and *apāna* is so called because it breathes by drawing down (*apakarṣaṇa*) through downward movement within the body; and *samāna* is so called because it breathes with equality (*samatā*) by equalizing [the vital force] throughout all the limbs; and *udāna* is so called because it breathes upward (*ut*) and all around (*samantāt*).

Because it moves upward (*ūrdhvam*) in association with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it is called *udāna*; and because it moves specifically (*viśeṣeṇa*) everywhere (*ā samantāt*) throughout all the vital points (*marmasu*) that support living beings, it is called *vyāna*. Thus, the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are generally five, and this constitutes the fivefold reality of wind (*vāyutattva*). Likewise, [they are located] in the stomach, mouth, ears, heart, and nose.

Space is the sky-principle (*nabhas-tattva*) in five ways; thus, by this division, the five elements exist fivefold within the body. Through them, the accomplishment of the fourteen-fold creation of beings occurs within the fourteen worlds (*bhuvana*), wherein the divine womb (*devayoni*) is eightfold, the animal womb (*tiryagyoni*) is fivefold, and the human state (*mānuṣya*) is singlefold. Thereafter—

Beyond the creation of the elements are the bodies of those qualified for instruction; "two-legged" means those who move or proceed by means of two [feet], being bipeds who are the essential recipients of the teaching. These very five elements, through their primary quality of the pentad of qualities (*pañcaguṇa*), are designated as the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
The intellect, the organs of action, and the senses are composed of the elements (bhūta) alone, being specific forms of one's own body;

the internal organs have those very elements as their cause; and the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas are combined, constituting the primordial nature (prakṛti), which is the innate, established substratum of the person (puruṣa). [In the Kha manuscript, the reading is "prakṛtipuruṣasya."]
As the scripture states: "The Lord, being formless and characterized by bliss, abides therein. (7–8)
Thus ends the second chapter in the Mahānayaprakāśa composed by the venerable teacher Śitikaṇṭhācārya. || 2 ||
The Illumination of the Great Way (Mahānayaprakāśa)
Now begins the third chapter.

(p. 36) Having thus described the creations of the Supreme Lord and Brahmā, he now proceeds with the subject matter at hand—the nature of the Great Purpose (*mahārtha*)—for which this entire undertaking was begun.
[It is conjectured— that here there must have been one root verse which appears to be missing from the section of the commentary below;
furthermore, the intent of that commentary does not cohere with the distinct meaning expressed in the subsequent verse.]
Thus it is inferred. || 1 ||

Now, what is this so-called "Great Purpose" (mahārtha)? Is it merely the recollection of the specific arrangement of the wheels and the Mistress of the Wheels? No, it is not that; we say that the Great Purpose is the immersion into the state of non-dual consciousness (cidadvaya). And thus: of those things perceivable by the five senses...
Among such objects as the *ṣaḍja* note, a garment, a cart, a mat, bark, smoke, and so forth— among those perceptible by a single sense organ,
such as the lute, the flute, the drum, and others— even though they are distinct, that which is called "perceptibility by the auditory faculty" [remains common].

It should be understood that there is only one [consciousness] which follows all; the distinction is twofold with respect to its own cognitions, and likewise, the non-difference of the objects of knowledge is the third [point]; similarly, there is non-difference among cognitions, whether they reside in a single sense organ or reside in multiple sense organs.

The fourth and fifth [points] concern the mutual [relationship] in every respect; the sixth non-difference is that the genus of cognition—whether residing in a single sense organ or residing in multiple sense organs—is in its ultimate reality the knower alone; and the knowers, each individually, have as their sole nature the state of being a knower.

The seventh [point] is that they are to be understood as merely possessing the nature of knowers— [in the Ka manuscript, the reading is "each one has the supreme reality of being a knower"]— and the eighth is that these knowers experience a state consisting of supreme non-duality through their consciousness-nature (cinmaya-rūpa) within the Supreme Subject (parapramātṛ). Thus—

May this non-duality, established in every way, be designated by the term "the Great Purpose" (mahārtha), consisting in the non-forgetfulness of the non-dual consciousness throughout all states. || 1 ||
Furthermore:
Whatever consciousness each living being possesses—whether it be blue, yellow, pleasure, or pain—arises as a self-equalized, equanimous flavor, corresponding exactly to its own particular nature. (2)

It brings together [all things] as a single consciousness, which is the universal nature, the Great Being (mahāsattā), designated as the equilibrium of consciousness (citsāmarasya), and whose essential form is peace; that alone is the supreme place of rest, the unique abode of the ultimate Goddess. Its slight swelling is the nature of pure consciousness alone.

Pervading both existence and non-existence, capable of being designated as both real and unreal— as expressed in the Upaniṣadic words, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" and "In the beginning, this was Non-being alone"—
she is the cause of the nourishment of the entire cosmic manifestation, its pervasive substratum, and its destroyer.
She who moves within the Great Family (Mahākulacāriṇī) is thus the place of rest; as the scripture says:
[In the manuscript *ka* at line 5, the reading is *samañī*; in the manuscript *ka* at line 4, the reading is *isa taptā*.]
The power of consciousness is stainless and pure, devoid of external perception;
established in the nature of Śiva’s true being, it is indeed renowned as the "Inexplicable" (Anākhyā).

Thus, this supreme speech (parāvāk), which possesses infinite powers individually, moves within the moving and the non-moving, is of the nature of the Self, follows the third stage, consists of the universe, and shines forth as consciousness from that Akula-nature; and so says the scripture:
By the power of its unfolding, the procreative Will arises;
that is the supreme, primordial emission, which is called the Pervasive One (Vyāpinī).
Wherever that desire suddenly falls upon an external object, its chewing [of that object] is called by the name "Sthiti" (Abiding); she is proclaimed as Samanā.
Having taken up its own essential nature, it is withdrawn through indifference toward that [nature];
and withdrawal occurs through the contraction of expansion by virtue of the transmental state (*unmanā*).

Thus, for whichever being— be they of superior, middling, or inferior kind— whatever [cognition] arises through whichever channel of the senses, or through that born of mental construction, in whatever manner, whether in the form of blue, yellow, and so forth, or in the form of mental pleasure and pain, or in the form of what is to be abandoned, what is to be adopted, or what is to be disregarded— that [is it].

In accordance with the path to be described hereafter, one becomes a vessel for the sequence in every respect; that very state is proclaimed by those who know the method as "the Great Sequence" (Mahākrama). || 2 ||
He says that very thing:
"The stages of each respective knowledge exist from the beginning through the middle to the end;
they consist of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal, with the beginning and end being equalized. (3)
For here, when a hundred lotus petals are pierced by a single effort simultaneously through the movement of extremely subtle and subtler temporal parts,

there is a contact with the initial, middle, and final portions of each individual petal; thus, by piercing the hundred petals in a single partless moment (*niraṃśakṣaṇa*), [the process is completed].

The piercing of the three hundred planes occurs; thus, even within a subtle expansion of consciousness (*saṃvit*), there arises a triad of planes for each, and the expansion of consciousness occurs in its proper place. Likewise, the arising, abiding, and dissolution of consciousness are necessarily present everywhere, and even the arising is distinguished by its beginning, middle, and end.

In three ways; likewise, persistence (*sthiti*) is also threefold in form—arising, persisting, and subsiding—and similarly, withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) also occurs in exactly three ways: proceeding, having proceeded, and being quiescent. And thus, this arising, which is non-different from itself, is threefold; persistence is threefold; and withdrawal is threefold.
Thus is the ninefold existence. And therein, beginning from the prior limit of the desire to arise (*uditsā*),

within the triadic nature of each of arising, persistence, and withdrawal, there exists as the pervasive reality until the final limit of withdrawal a single, all-pervading, infinite, and boundless essence of the Goddess.

Thus, this is the meaning of the sequence (*krama*): at the beginning, middle, and end, the establishment of that knowledge as a sequence appears through the distinction of stages (*bhūmikā*) by virtue of the equality of its beginning and end;

and it appears through the processes of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal, as well as through other modes of expression such as the forms of attainment, acquisition, and satisfaction. [Variant reading in manuscript *kha*: ...]

The reading is "attainment of affliction through other states of being. [6] Or else, it is introduced everywhere according to the instruction by others; and that Great Sequence (mahākrama), as previously stated, is defined as fourfold together with the first. || 3 ||

Now, in order to apply the meaning of the sequence through the terminology of emanation and so forth, and to negate the fivefold meaning through the terminology of arising and so forth, he says: "In the experience of the [state] beyond the Creator (Iṣṭyājī), there is the prescription of the various divisions of the arising of the [spiritual] power."
In the manifestation of the path of coming and going, he is the one who destroys the pervasive lords. || 4 ||
In this form of the specific northern *ghoravallī*, which is designated as "Great Bliss" (*mahānanda*), it is conventionally defined as the "fourfold meaning" (*catuṣṭayārtha*); that is,
the very fourfold [process] beginning with emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) is asserted as the meaning of the sequence.

What room is there for the five [categories] consisting of arising (*udaya*), manifestation (*avabhāsa*), relishing (*carvaṇa*), the time of swallowing (*kālagrāsa*), and repose (*viśrānti*)? For the arrangement of the other five categories belonging to the other *pīṭhas* is well known; however, it is not the case that the fourth is cessation (*virati*)—namely attainment (*prāpti*) and satisfaction (*tṛpti*)—and the fifth is repose (*viśrānti*).
To explain that meaning, it is said: "Āvana" refers to the place from which both descent (*avatāra*) and withdrawal (*pratyastamaya*) are perceived;
thus, there is only one all-pervasive reality for the various classes of cognition.

Consequently, what difference is there between cessation (*virati*) and repose (*viśrānti*), or between the repose of the swallowing of time (*kālagrāsa*) and the ineffable form (*anākhyarūpa*)? For the swallowing of time is indeed withdrawal.
According to the scripture,
the primordial power is all-pervasive; she abides as Samanā during the maintenance of the work of creation,
and she is to be known as Unmanā during dissolution, for she is the first power and is omnipresent.
Thus it is said.
Furthermore: "How indeed could there be a manifestation through an effect once [the world] has ceased?
For that which is liberated from the three types of effects is proclaimed to be inexpressible."
Thus, even that which is seen as the meaning of the five verses is of the nature of the expansion of the pentad beginning with Vāmeśī; therefore, there is no fault. Now, [the sequence is]:
Vṛ— — — — — —, Kaulī, Śvetā, Sthairya, and Saṃhṛti-caṇḍī.
Śuṣkā, Kālavināśa, Viśrānti, and Bhairava.

Thus, the meaning of the sequence (*krama*) alone has been explained in five ways. However, this is stated too briefly; for in this system, it is declared that there is an explanation of the meaning of the fourfold set. Therefore, the Great Sequence (*mahākrama*) consists of exactly four forms.
As for the "fivefold meaning," which arises from the worship of the fifth form, Bhairava, in other traditions:
How could that which has been taught be otherwise? Thus, exactly as it was stated is superior. || 4 ||
He speaks in a pair of verses (*yugalaka*) to elaborate upon that very point:
"When the supreme power (*paraśakti*) vibrates within the nature of Śiva, it remains outside as the sprout of pervasion (*vyāpana*).
When it arises in the vibration of *samanā* facing [Śiva], it culminates in the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of existence. (5)
If one turns away from the true meaning of existence and shifts toward the external, that is the destruction of the mind;
likewise, by facing the abode of Śambhu, there is the remedy that cannot be described.

(A pair of verses) Power is indeed of the very nature of Śiva and not a separate entity; thus, the reality of the thing designated as Śiva and the reality designated as Power is one and the same, and there is nothing new here. In this way, Power is primordial.

That [power] which is by nature vibrating, oriented toward external objects, and becomes the recipient of the designation "emanation" (sṛṣṭi) through its pervasive state— when that very same [power], by means of an intense internal absorption and withdrawal into the interior, takes the form of *samanā*, it is called "stasis" (sthiti). Thereafter, having assimilated the essential nature of all objective phenomena (*bhāva*) into itself, its nature turns back and it becomes the state of *unmanā*.

That very [power] becomes designated as withdrawal (*saṃhāra*); furthermore, that same primordial power, being without limiting adjuncts (*anupādhi*), is inexpressible, yet—as before—it is described as having the form of Śakti within the nature of Śambhu.
By means of this removal—that is, by resorting to rest through the abandonment of limiting adjuncts—[it returns to its original state].
According to the scripture, when consciousness possesses desire, it is there that power is known as *sṛṣṭi* (emanation);
from that comes *sthiti* (maintenance), then *nivṛtti* (cessation) and *saṃhāra* (reabsorption); and the *anākhyā* (the Ineffable) pervades the beginning, the end, and the middle.
Thus, the unnameable, supreme, pure Consciousness is held to be its Will, which is Emanation;
its Immersion in the middle is Maintenance, and its reversal is Withdrawal.
Thus,
creation follows one's will, and persistence is the wonder of the mind;
by the absence of these two comes withdrawal, at the end of which lies the system of the deities.
Thus: "In this way,
the differentiation of sequence within the single stream of consciousness regarding its own object—
that which is the meaning of sequence through will, knowledge, and action— is what is designated as such."
Likewise,
the progressive transition of a single power through its fourfold divisions—
namely creation, maintenance, dissolution, and the nameless— is proclaimed as "Krama."
Thus ends the corroboration for the sake of understanding the sequence of the meaning. 5–6.
(p. 46) Now, one might raise the doubt: "Is this consciousness indeed one and the same, or are these merely distinct stages arising from specific experiences? To dispel this doubt, he says:
"The stream of consciousness, which flows with a constant and unceasing current, has ten times ten remaining surges."
The lords of the quarters, beginning with the East, are mounted upon their respective vehicles, each possessing five tusks.
Consciousness alone, appearing in the form of blue and other objects, flows like a stream with a turbulent and unstable current;
yet, when its nature is subsequently withdrawn, it is perceived as having a natural form that spreads forth, moving from the foremost to the foremost.

This is the differentiation within the unconditioned consciousness caused by limiting adjuncts such as creation and the like; and that [consciousness] manifests as fourfold according to the distinction of the stages (bhūmikās).

Even while being perceived as one, they touch [the object] in six ways; through the distinction between cognition and action, they attain the state of twelve rays. And through the superimposition of the five Vāmeśīs upon that [group of twelve], there is a fivefold division consisting of individual channels (prativāha), as will be described hereafter. || 7 ||
In order to provide rest for the very meaning already explained, he says:
"O Paśu, behold! This great treasure here consists of the knowledge and the knowable of both aquatic and terrestrial beings;
those who have realized the non-dual state of their own and others' auspiciousness and blessings in both worlds. (8)

Let this great purpose be seen—let it be directly realized through the direct perception of one's own experience. Where? To this he says: "in water, in the forest," meaning among both the stationary and the moving; for it has been stated that when the activity of the senses expands—that is, when an object becomes the domain of sensory function—it is not difficult to describe its immediate presence before the senses, as indicated by the word "paśya" (behold) regarding the object.

What is called "knowability" (*jñeyatva*) is not an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), but rather a property residing in cognition (*jñāna*) consisting in dependence upon cognition. For an entity's intrinsic nature cannot be dependent on something else; therefore, so-called knowability—which is a function of cognition (the reading *jñeyavṛtti* is found in manuscript *kha*)—is non-different from cognition itself, and cognition likewise...
The outward-turning state of the self—that which was praised by me myself in the *Stotramālā*—is seen as follows:

"Just as on a painted canvas both [the inner and outer] are one within the single cloth, so too the multitude of bodies is outside [of the Self]; yet the consciousness of that [Self], whose light is indivisible, knows the interior. (p. 48)
The nature of knowledge belongs to the rays of consciousness that possess unimpeded senses.
Thus, outward-turnedness belongs to one who is incomplete and agitated by longing;

therefore, it has been said that for the complete Self there is the state of being established in knowledge (*jñānavṛttitā*). This means that having contemplated both knowledge and the object of knowledge (*jñāna-jñeya*) as being nothing other than the very nature of the Self, the Self is consequently completely full.

The practice becomes one that has attained great purpose; this very thing is non-contradictory to both worlds, auspicious, and a blessing for both oneself and others—that which is called the meditation on non-duality (advayībhāvanā).
This is the true nature of the meaning of the vision. Thus, the nature of the great purpose is [established] through the lineage in the supreme seat (pīṭhavara).
That it exists in a hidden manner is indicated here by the compound [guhyasamāja]. || 8 ||
He says this very thing:
"O Lord, at the seat of Pavana, you were instructed in the silence of the supreme reality, both external and internal;
filled with compassion for all beings during your incarnations, you are the one who has transcended the accumulation of ritual actions."

Having received instruction at the supreme seat (*pīṭha*) of the illustrious Goddess Makārā, the venerable Jñānanetranātha directly realized the true nature of the primordial Goddess as she exists both externally and internally; being filled with compassion for living beings, he has now emitted that very realization through both exposition and worship for the sake of the Krama tradition. Thus.
This is the indication of the chapters; that very [subject] is now introduced. || 9 ||
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Mahānayaprakāśa* composed by the venerable teacher Śitikaṇṭha. || 3 ||
Now begins the fourth arising. Now, the wheel of the sacred seats (*pīṭhacakra*): Oḍḍiyāna is the seat, Śacī is the cremation ground, Ullasana is the field, and Melāpu is the meeting place.
In the contemplation of the experience of the *yāgu* (gruel), there is likewise the obstacle of the fivefold non-renunciation. || 1 ||

Uḍḍiyāna: because of the surging of Śakti at the sacred seat (pīṭha), [it is so called] since in this sacred seat of Āvaṭha, the Śakti of the residents is seen to be constantly and abundantly "flown up" (uḍḍīnā)—that is, manifesting. Thus, the sacred seat equal to Āvaṭha is defined as Oḍḍiyāna.

And outside, that *praṇava-pīṭha* is the locus of the deity’s convention (*devatā-saṃketa*). Within that essential nature of the *āvaṭha*, the *pīṭhas*, *śmaśānas*, *kṣetras*, *melāpas*, and *yāgas* are designated by way of division according to the sequence to be described, based on the authority of the experiential stages (*anubhūyamāna-bhūmikā*). What indeed is their [status] here?
Denial. || 1 ||
To introduce this very point, he says:

Know that very Pīṭha to be the one who adorns all things, formless and of the nature of wind, moving both within oneself and others; it is the seat of consciousness, the source of the channels, and the Liṅga of the head. (2)
That very seat (*pīṭha*) is, in every respect, the ornament of all the great systems (*mahānaya*),

because it serves as their foundation; thus, one should understand that this [seat], which is synonymous with *asvara* and *praṇava*, possesses a "seat-like" nature common to both itself and other moving beings (*jaṅgama*), within those seats in which the conscious (*cinmaya*)...

The Lord in the form of the *liṅga* is the head; thus, by virtue of being the locus of the organs of action, the body is the sacred seat (*pīṭha*), and because the head is of the nature of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), it is the *liṅga*. Consequently, whatever consists of the five elements is the site of establishment for those five [categories], such as the sacred seats, cremation grounds, and so forth.

"The abode of the gods": just as one has regard for and devotion toward one's own body, so too should one have toward the bodies of all living beings; just as the self consisting of consciousness is the presiding lord of one's own body, so too is the single self consisting of consciousness within all bodies; and that [self] is indeed one, like the reflection of the sun in various water-vessels.

It should be understood as residing in all living beings. In this way, the realization of the *liṅga* and the *pīṭha* everywhere should be meditated upon with distinction—thus is the nature of the *pīṭha*. || 2 ||
Explaining according to the manner in which it was thus stated, he says:
The body of the Piśāca is the fuel for the fire of the three worlds; the Piśāca is the body of the Kali age.
When the wheel of consciousness dissolves into the tenth [state], this is the seat of the three Miśrāṇas. (3)
"An entity is like grass when touched by the fire of consciousness"— thus, the cemetery is the withdrawal of the objects of the senses once they have become the objects of one's own experience;
and the vital breaths, which are the devourers, touch the body of Kālī and there find their rest.
The second cremation ground is the devouring by Time (*kālagrāsa*), wherein the entire wheel of mental activity dissolves in the thirteenth [palate];

the third cremation ground is the Great Withdrawal (*mahāsaṃhāra*). Of these, the first is the devouring of the object by the goddess of one's own rays; the second is the subsiding of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the *kula* itself upon the plane of non-breath (*aprāṇabhūmi*).
The third [stage] is the subsiding of all mental fluctuations into the body of Śrī Kālikā; externally, that is the nature of the Karavīra. || 3 ||

Now, regarding the true nature of the Kṣetrapāla: the body of the field is called the protector of the field; this is the designation. He who causes the world to move by the flow of the unstruck sound (nāda) is the one whose form is beyond description. 4.
The field is the body; its protector and presiding authority is the Self (ātman), as it is sung:
"O son of Kuntī, this body is called the field;
he who knows this is called the Knower of the Field by those who understand it."

Thus [it is said]. And of that [field], there are four divisions of planes (*bhūmikā*) wherein that very same Supreme Form (*parārūpa*) is characterized by three modes of speech; those four planes are as follows:

[first] the form of *paśyantī*, which consists of the non-sound of the unstruck resonance (*anāhatanāda*); [second] that which, due to being agitated by conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), functions through the activity of the mind (*mānasa-vyāpāra*).

The Self is the sustainer of the world, moving it by impelling it, thus being the Jagaccālaka (the Mover of the World) in the form of Madhyamā; it is the employer of the sixty-four phonemes and the syllables of the Vaikharī speech, thus being in the form of Vaikharī; and as the presiding deity over these three modes of speech, it is in the form of the Fourth, the Parā-vāc.

It is the place for the exhaustion of the class of objects to be known; thus, even externally at the site of convention, the Lord of the Field (kṣetrādhipa) residing in the sacred seat (pīṭha), who is intent on guarding against obstacles from both his own and others, should be worshipped as being most powerful. || 4 ||
Now he speaks of the meeting (*melāpa*):
"O Aka, O Vāhadeva, at the time of the absence of afflictions (*akaleśa*), the assembly (*melāpu*) occurs in its own domain;
at every moment, O Ādideva, by your command, the collection of assemblies (*melāpakalāpu*) resides in many sacred seats (*pīṭha*). (5)

Each individual goddess of the senses, without effort and by her own spontaneity, brings about a union within each respective domain through the presiding presence of the Primordial Goddess; thus occurs the union of the sense-deities situated in the *āvaṭha* and *pīṭha* seats, and that [union] is distinct for each— this is the state of the twelfth.
Having become a bundle. || 5 ||
Now he describes the nature of the sacrifice:
"O Goddess, O Bhairava who drags away time, look upon this great sacrifice!
The mind is the vessel, the 'mine-ness' is the sacrificial pap; attract it, drink it, and let water be the offering. (6)

The supreme goddess Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, for the sake of the complete cessation of all mental fluctuations during the great sacrifice (mahāyāga) of Bhairava, draws forth the mind, intellect, and ego from the sacrificial pap (caru) and offers them; thereafter, she, who encircles the vital breaths on all sides, [offers] her own supreme vital breaths [according to the Kha manuscript].

[The reading: Clinging to her surrounding embrace for the sake of identity with her own Self, and not out of greed for the morsel [of objects], she who dissolves the universe—thus dissolving even those vital breaths (*prāṇas*)—being by nature pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), perceives her husband Kuleśvara as unsatisfied; becoming agitated, she [offers] that very Self, which is pure consciousness, to him.

"He offers it as a sacrificial gift to Bhairava"—thus the middle sacrifice (*madhyayāga*) is threefold: gross, subtle, and supreme; and this is the ground of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*). And so it is said in the *Śrīrājikā*:
"When the Lord of Kula, having consumed the entire universe without exception, has not yet attained full satiation..."
Then the goddess offered her own body as an oblation here to the Lord of the Kula.

Thus, having offered those four, she becomes agitated and causes herself to become one in flavor (*samarasībhāvayati*) with the form of the supreme speech (*parāvāk*); this is the meaning of the offering. In this way, through the offering of intellect, ego, mind, and breath to the Goddess who is intent on devouring them completely, there arises an agitation of the self.
The sacrifice consisting of the consumption of the five sacrificial pap-offerings (caru) in a state of aesthetic unification (sāmarasya) has been prescribed. || 6 ||
He concludes this very point among others:
"The Great Hero possesses great power and great majesty;
he is the one who has abandoned existence and attained nirvāṇa, the discerning one who has reached all things, yet he does not cling to the highest state. (7)

Thus, this [teaching] called the *pīṭha* is of great significance (*mahārtha*). Because it belongs to the tradition of the Great Significance (*mahārthasaṃpradāya*), it should be understood as the bodily (*śārīra*) and internal (*antaraṅga*) "five-fold flow" (*pañcavāha*), which contains within it the Great Sequence (*mahākrama*) and consists of the fourfold meaning; or rather, the Great Sequence itself is the Great Significance. Therefore...

Whether as the foundation for worldly existence (*lokayātrā*), or as the state of rest in the condition of liberation (*nirvāṇa*), or in the form of the Unconditioned Mistress of the Left (*nirupādhivāmeśī*), or even through the Great Sequence (*mahākrama*)—this very Mahārtha exists manifest in many ways through its divisions; it should be recognized as the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). In truth, however:

Beginning from the *pīṭhacakra* up to the end of the *samayavidyā*, the Great Purpose (*mahārtha*) itself becomes manifest through an equal sovereignty, just as will be explained; let this be contemplated, for herein there is no distinction between the trivial and the essential. Thus ends the nature of the *pīṭhacakra*. || 7 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Mahānayaprakāśa composed by the venerable teacher Śitikaṇṭha. || 4 ||

(p. 57) Now begins the fifth chapter. Alternatively, the tradition of Vāmeśī is now revealed, wherein this introduction is made by way of a summary [the reading "sarvākṣepeṇa" is found in manuscript ka].
The Guru and the Goddess said: "O brother, the deities of the Akathiya [Akathita] lineage are mutually devoted to one another;
where the Ocean of Milk is, there indeed is the dance of the minds of others. || 1 ||

The lineage of gurus (*gurukrama*) and the lineage of deities (*devatākrama*) are in every way the presiding and inner-moving authority; however, within the lineage of deities, the lineage of deities itself is subsumed in successive stages,
because the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) is of such a nature that each individual deity [is contained] between the Guru and the deity.
By acting as the presiding deity in each successive stage, pervading one after another without interruption,

it maintains a continuous connection with this state of vision; therefore, whichever single deity is worshipped from whichever position within the circle, that very deity, once worshipped, through its presiding presence, becomes like the final goddess of the meditated mandala.
"It becomes the giver of fruit"—this refers to the fruit of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Just as even drinking a single mouthful from the Ocean of Milk yields the fruit of drinking nectar, it has been said:
"Even a mere span of Brahman does not transcend its universal form and is beyond conceptualization."
Thus: in the wheel of the seats (*pīṭhacakra*), the Śākinīs, the leaders of the wheels (*cakranāyikās*),
the Vāmeśīs, and the deities of the transmission (*kramadevīs*) are pervasive, each succeeding one more so than the last.
