Pervasion is the gradual veiling by the subsequent [energies] according to their respective order;
thus, pervasion in the wheel of the seats (pīṭhacakra) is prescribed as fivefold.
The host of Śākinīs resides in the three abodes with three [groups] each; [according to the Ka-pu manuscript, the reading is "residing in the four abodes"].
Through the two, by means of the pervasion of the Cakreśvarī, they are the deities of the Vāmeśīs.
The meaning of succession is pervaded internally by a subsequent meaning of succession;
such is this division of pervasion, which extends everywhere both externally and internally.

Each individual deity exists by presiding over the one situated below it— namely, the deity situated below— in the form of its power (*śakti*), not in its manifest form; thus, each and every one [of them].
Other superior deities exist presiding over that manifestation in the form of their respective powers; therefore,

that goddess Māheśvarī is like the presiding deity of the ocean of milk, from whom various thirsty beings may drink— either by a single, undivided vision, or, due to its indivisibility, by many mere handfuls from whichever side they approach.
Then, by means of the heart-captivating sound produced by the waves,
the refreshing touch, the wondrous form, the nectar-like taste, and the divine fragrance, it generates a state that gratifies all five senses; thus, this is the supreme [state].

This is a specific pervasion (*vyāpti-viśeṣa*). Thus, first of all, this wheel of seats (*pīṭhacakra*) consists of five [elements]: the seats and so forth, the cremation grounds (*śmaśāna*), the field-protectors (*kṣetrapāla*), the meeting places (*melāpa*), and the sacrifices (*yāga*). These are presided over by the five elements known as earth, which exist in the form of power (*śakti*). This is their sequence of abodes (*dhāmakrama*), as well as that of the entire syllable.
And it is pervaded by their digits—the Mothers Raudrī, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Ambā—thus is the sequence of the five phonemes;
and likewise, there is the well-spoken verse of the Siddha:
Earth, water, fire, air, and ether.

Thus, this is the sequence of the phonemes (*varṇakrama*); likewise, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been established by Raudrī, Īśvarī, and the others, in due order, as being the very nature of consciousness (*saṃvidrūpatā*). This is the sequence of consciousness (*saṃvitkrama*) for those seats (*pīṭha*) and other locations.
Similarly, there is the mantric pervasion (*māntrī vyāpti*) by means of the five groups of syllables (*pañcapiṇḍārṇa*) beginning with *ma* and ending with *kha*. And thus:
In the Kula-sūtras it is stated that [the reality] designated by the Kulapīṭhas, Kṣetras, and so forth, as well as the five Piṇḍas and the Praṇava,
belongs to that consciousness which is identified with the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) and whose nature is the manifestation of all things.
The body is the abode of the self, being its common substratum;

therefore, the body itself is the seat (*pīṭha*) of the *praṇava*. Furthermore, the name *praṇava* is applied externally to the seat because it resembles the *praṇava* due to the fivefold encircling of the configuration of the navel.

Because it arose first, this is its name. Likewise, Oḍḍiyāna is so called because it begins with the syllable *o*; and due to the abundance of the manifestation (*ullāsa*) of power (*śakti*), it is Oḍḍiyāna in the sense of "manifestation. Thus, the designation "Oḍḍiyāna" represents the pervasion between the signifier and the signified. And likewise:

They are presided over by the processes of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal; such is the sequence of consciousness (*saṃvitkrama*). From the abode of the Goddess (*devīdhāman*), all five have emerged simultaneously (*akrameṇa*) and are established in that very place;
they have her as their nature, she is their sole life-force, and they rest within her—such is the sequence of the unobscured abode (*nirāvaraṇadhāmakrama*). Now:

The pervasion of the Vāmeśīs: This supreme *pañcavāha* is that pervasive one for whom there is no fixed location due to its specific individual levels of consciousness; whereas the other *pañcavāha* has fixed locations extending from the ears and other senses, and possesses fixed functions—it is of this [latter] that the term *pañcavāha* is used.

The worldly convention [is said to exist] either through delusion or by way of metaphorical designation; [in the Ka-pu manuscript, the reading is "through joy (modāt) or by way of metaphorical designation, it is indeed not prohibited"]. That [worldly convention] is indeed prohibited. || 1 ||
Now, through six metaphors, the true nature of the wheel of Vāmeśī is revealed:
in the totality of the existence of Vāmeśī, she exists as the state of the sense-faculties (buddhīndriya) which are like shaven heads;
she exists as the state of the motor-faculties (karmendriya) which are like staff-bearers; and she exists as the activity of knowledge through the movement toward its own objects.
Thus is the reading. || 2 ||

The one and only supreme power of consciousness (*parā cicchakti*), whose essential nature is great existence (*mahāsattā*)— or, according to the *Ka* manuscript, whose nature is pure consciousness and tranquility (*cinmātraśānta*)— possesses a slight swelling (*kiṃciducchūnatā*) which pervades both being and non-being, is capable of being designated as both existent and non-existent, and is the cause of the manifold expansion of the universe (*viśvaprapañca*).

The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the pervasive, withdrawing power (*śakti*) that dwells in the Great Kula; she is the resting place, whose nature is *akula*, whose essence is radiant vibration (*sphurattā*), and who exists in the form of a wave (*ūrmi*). This [power] is Parā-vāk, who abides within the domain of manifestation (*parigraha*), who moves within the mobile and immobile, whose form is the Self (*ātman*), who follows the third stage (*bhūmikā*), and who consists of the entire universe.

It shines, whose own innate expansion—situated within the *kula*—manifests in three ways: by way of the sequence of resonance (*rāva*), by way of the sequence of the arising of power (*śakti*), and by way of the sequence of the unfolding of the radiance of light;
and that sequence of resonance is tenfold, being both unmanifest (as the unstruck sound, *anāhata*, the resonance, etc. and manifest (as the struck sound, *hata*), even though it is infinite.
The twelvefold form of the syllable *oṃ*, beginning with the vowel *a* and *u* and ending with *unmanā*, is the nature of its constituent parts;
and the emergence of Śakti occurs at the root of birth, where the knot called Māyā constitutes the bondage of birth.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
The five knots situated in the *kāraṇa* [cakras] have been proclaimed;
the knot known as Indhikā is Śiva, who causes the cessation of the two paths of the mind.
Above that is the one named Dīpikā, and above that is the Bindu;
then follows the great knot called Nāda, and beyond that is the Śakti-knot.
Thus, the expansion of rays is limited to twelve knots;
and consisting of the sixfold group of cognitive faculties accompanied by the intellect, and the sixfold group of active faculties together with the vital breath—
these being the nature of the sovereign goddesses of the instruments situated upon the twelve-fold path of the fingers— it is composed of thirty-six principles.

The first is the expansion of that power which abides as its appropriation; and she, the primordial goddess thus described as the supreme, is manifested everywhere throughout all three types of twelve-fold stations by the expansion of her own majesty [the *ka* manuscript reads "by the expansion of her own nature"]. In every respect, she is entirely present.

Shining forth as the all-pervasive, it reveals within that expansion of the Supreme Goddess belonging to the Kula, the wheel of the Karaneśvarīs— which consists of the sequential emergence of the rays of the rising breath (*rāva*)— and therein, within each individual form of a Karaneśvarī.

By virtue of its manifestation as the pervader of the totality of that form, the pentad of Vāmeśvarīs—which is the universal form—pervades everything; it has been explained in its entirety and in sequence according to each specific function.
And thus, that which first unfolds as the void, designated as Vāmeśvarī, is what flashes forth.

He dwells within the stage of the first unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of those twelve sovereigns of the instruments (*karaṇeśvarī*). And thus, he completely pervades all the spheres of authority of those sovereigns of the instruments, which are denoted by the term *khecarī*. And the third...

That which is called Bhūcarī presides over the entire twelvefold individual objects of those very Karaṇeśvarīs. Likewise, the fourth form, Vāmeśvarī— designated as Saṃhārabhakṣiṇī— is characterized by the withdrawal (*pratyāharaṇa*) of the enjoyment of objects.

It pervades those twelve stages (*bhūmikā*)— which consist of the withdrawal (*pratyāharaṇa*) of each respective object— in a general, all-encompassing, and exhaustive manner. And it pervades the fifth stage,
designated as the state of Raudrīśvarī, which is the primordial unfolding of the stage of consciousness experienced externally.

Relying upon her own essential nature— which is precisely her own unobscured nature— she pervades in an all-encompassing form like Ādidevī; for like Ādidevī, she is the fixed, inherent foundation within the *kula* of the Vāmeśvarīs, who are all-pervasive and whose nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*).

There is no such thing; however, that conventional usage which distinguishes the respective domains based on the forms of the substrates of the senses, such as the ear and so forth, is figurative (*aupacārika*) and not real (*vāstava*). Now, is it not well-known in the world that the *pañcavāha* consists of the five goddesses who are the mistresses of the instruments (*karaṇeśvarī*)? This is not so—the six mistresses of the instruments constitute one group, which is a manifestation (*vivarta*) of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), while the other...

And since [the organs] are of the nature of transformations of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), there are twelve Lords of the Instruments (*karaṇeśvarī*); if the pentad of the mind (*manas*) is separated from among them, only seven remain—so how can there be the conventional usage of the number "twelve rays" (*marīci*)? For the rays, such as hearing and the rest, established in their fixed locations, would be devoid of their own respective functions.
How could those [energies] such as Vāmā and the others—who are like those born blind regarding the activities of others—be considered "mistresses" (īśī)?

As for the common designation in the world of these rays of the ears and other senses as the "five winds" (pañcavāha), that is conceived of through their presiding deities; and thus, there is no distinction among the entire circle of deities who are the rays.

Vāmeśī is one alone as the pervasive [power] whose body is the first unfolding (*unmeṣa*); then, having fallen into the station of the instruments (*karaṇa*), she is designated in her totality as that very Khecarī; and from that state, having become solidified and extending her feet by presiding over the multitude of objects, she is Bhūcarī, who effects the devouring of objects.

"Internally and externally she is the devourer of the withdrawal [of the universe]"; thus, having established her sovereignty both internally and externally, she sustains the course of worldly existence; and through the terrifying of duality, she is Raudreśvarī, whose very nature is formidable, yet she shines forth in a stainless form. In this way, each one among the twelve is a Mistress of the Organs (*karaṇeśvarī*).
It is empowered by five or five Vāmeśīs through the process of *utpattikrama*;

thus, sixty stages (*bhūmikās*) are indicated for the twelve [deities], and all that expansion is to be contemplated as belonging solely to the Primordial Goddess (*Ādidevī*). In this way, the one supreme power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is [manifested] in relation to the sequence consisting of its own future expansion.
Having obtained the designation of Ādidevī, she possesses a limitation to fivefold number due to the differentiation of the stages (*bhūmikā*);
yet, even while existing in that state, she remains none other than her original, innate nature (*sahajasvarūpa*) which has never fallen away.
Furthermore, within these five stages, there is an assigned relationship of primary and secondary importance.
Due to the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as Khecarī and others, which are characterized solely by mental constructs (*saṃskāra*), this appears as if divided;
yet in reality, it is nothing but pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). This is the primordial vibration, designated by the term "First Mistress of the Left" (*ādyaspandita-prathamavāmeśī*).
Thus, it is neither deficient nor excessive in relation to Khecarī, Bhūcarī, Grāsakī, and Raudreśvarī.

The nature of pure consciousness alone is mutually of a single essence, like five stainless mirrors within one [mirror]; however, it appears as if diverse through the stages created by mere reflections, whereas in reality, it is so within the supreme ground of consciousness and within its own fivefold pure nature.

Likewise, even within the outward expansion of the rays (*marīci*), in all three locations, there exists that which culminates in unity when perceived as the single, pure nature of consciousness alone; and this is the first expansion of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) of that Vāmeśvarī, containing within it the other power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).

Through the unfolding of the cognitive organs in the manner of a "shaven head" (muṇḍa), and the second [aspect], through the unfolding of the organs of action in the manner of a "staff" (daṇḍa)— which is the expansion of the power of action containing the power of knowledge— it sports, having assimilated its respective objects to itself. || 2 ||
Expanding upon this very point, he says in a pair of verses:

First, the goddess Śivā, the mistress of the left, having caused the wheel of hands to expand in the sky-farer (khecara), enjoys the food that is free from decay—the enjoyer of objects and the non-enjoyer of objects, who has become one with the earth-dweller (bhu-cara). || 3 ||

O Supreme Lord, whose form is both partless and with parts, fierce, moving, and playful; O Lord with eyes like those of a crow, do not depart from me! May you, who are the source of all forms, protect me! 4.
(The Couple:
That which is the first vibration from the form of supreme consciousness, which is the form of the Goddess, is Vāmeśvarī;
thereafter, having become solidified, it attains the state of a wave and falls into the doors of the senses.
That which is designated by the term *khecarī* (the sky-farer), because of its relative grossness, extends its "feet" further and,
engaging with object after object, becomes designated by the term *bhūcarī* (the earth-farer). And therein,
having assimilated object after object through the distinction of locations, it [attains] the *madhyamā* (intermediate state) by means of the internal-external form.

Having attained the stage, he becomes designated as *Saṃhārabhakṣiṇī*; yet, by touching the internal and external locations while sustaining the course of worldly life, he is defined as *Raudreśvarī* through the touch of both the partless (*niṣkala*) and the manifest (*sakala*) forms. In reality, however, the Supreme Goddess is like a crow’s eye, [perceiving] through a single expansion of consciousness.
It touches, in its very unmodified form, all three stages: the stage of origin which is the nature of pure consciousness alone, the stage of expansion, and the nature of the object itself. (3–4)
He says that very thing:
Seated upon the seats of Uḍḍiyāna, Jālandhara, and Pūrṇagiri, one should consume the sacrificial oblation (caru) with a mind free from worldly attachment;
having placed the feet within and without, one should perform the rites for the deities in the supreme current (para-ogha). || 5 ||

Thus described— attained to her station, immersed in the objects of the senses, having swallowed all states of being, and though possessing the form of the universe, yet having attained oneness— the primordial Goddess, according to the aforementioned method, unfolds fivefold through division; yet she remains, by her own indivisible state, with a body that is both partless and whole, fallen into the objects and devouring them within.
And it has been stated that by means of the entered *akāra*, she shines forth, pervading both internally and externally like the eye of a crow;

this too is enumerated as one (1). From the abode of Ādidevī, the supreme station, a single wave arises; divided among the channels of the internal sense-faculties, it attains the state of *icchā* (will), and through that sequence, it reaches the twelve locations of the sense-faculties.

The fallen emission is *khecarī* (2); immediately thereafter, penetrating its own object, through the immersion in that object, it has the nature of the state of *bhūcarī* (3); following that, having withdrawn the object, its nature being merely reverted, the fourth is *saṃhārabhakṣiṇī*, which has the nature of withdrawal (4).

Even beyond that, the pure state is one where the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of objects have ceased to persist, even when there remains only the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) of the shadow of objects previously assimilated as one's own. But the fifth state, which is terrible, consists of those very same impressions in their manifold forms; though they have not yet reached contact with future objects and exist in a form neither internal nor external, they pervade both the internal and the external, sustaining the course of worldly life.

*Raudreśvarī*—according to the supreme lineage (*para-ogha*) and the sequence of gurus—should be understood as the intended deity manifesting in each one’s own individual form. Now, the pervasion of the sequence of carriers (*vāhakrama-vyāpti*): where there is the pervasion of the abode (*dhāma-vyāpti*) through rest, that occurs in the center of the triangle named *Kulapadma*, which is the pervasion by the first goddess.

In the corner situated on the left is the pervasion of the fourth goddess; then, by returning once more, there is the pervasion of the fifth goddess, Raudreśī, in the central position, which here is the region of the head of the vowel-less (asvara) [letter]. Thus, the sequence of phonemes is presided over by the goddesses of the left through the pervasion of the vowel-less. Now, the sequence of consciousness (saṃvitkrama).

—By the initial vibration (*ādyaspanda*), the first goddess has entered the path of the senses; the second has fallen into the sphere of the objects (*viṣaya*); the third, having not yet assimilated those objects as her own, has turned back; the fourth, moreover, has touched the root-ground (*mūlabhūmi*) and, even externally, her expansion remains unmanifest (*avyakta*). What, then, is the fifth?—thus [it is asked].
The sequence of consciousness proceeds by way of the staff and the shaven head. Now, the sequence of the unobscured abode of these very [energies] is as follows:

she who vomits—that is, emits—the various forms of consciousness into the void is the Mistress of the Left (Vāmeśvarī) of the Void, whose nature is consciousness; she who moves in the "kha"—the sky of one's own nature—is likewise the Khecarī, whose essential form is the Supreme.

She who moves upon the plane of supreme reflective awareness (*paravimarśa*) is *Bhūcarī*; she who withdraws all this which has been projected forth is *Saṃhārabhakṣiṇī*; and she who, having first attained identity with the Great Void (*māhāvyoman*) in the form of *Vyomavāmeśvarī* as described, is *Raudrīśvarī*—this is the sequence of the unconditioned abode (*nirāvaraṇadhāmakrama*).

For the expansion of the Sky-farer (khecarī) is inclined toward the solar abode; the expansion of the Earth-farer (bhūcarī) is the expansion of the lunar abode; and the expansion of the Devourer of Withdrawal (saṃhārabhakṣiṇī) is the expansion of the fiery abode.
The expansions of the Primordial Goddess and the Final Goddess are the presiding deities of all the abodes. Thus is the sequence of the abodes (dhāmakrama). || 5 ||

(p. 72) Having thus described the essential nature of the Mistress of the Left, he speaks in a pair of verses (*yugalaka*) in order to investigate whether these [goddesses] are to be conceived as gurus or as deities.

O Pīḍa, contemplate the five auspicious [deities] consisting of the primordial God (Ādideva) according to their respective specific sequences; contemplate the five-armed one in the state of Guru, possessing a form as beautiful as that of the gods.
Having worshipped the various deities of the *dyuguru-mantra* according to the supreme meaning of the *āpa* [mantra], which has many divisions, || 7 ||
(A pair of verses:

The nature of the Primordial Goddess is indeed without distinction; if the nature of Vāmeśvarī is thus ascertained, what else is worshipped in the form of the deity who is the goal? This being so, such is the nature of the meaning of the future sequence.

This is the elaboration of that very point— it is logical— if it is asserted that the nature of this pentad of Vāmeśīs is precisely that of the lineage of gurus (*gurukrama*) which serves as the means (*upāya*). Then, what other distinct form, characterized as the goal (*upeya*), could there be for these deities beyond this very nature, such that they would be designated by this pentad of gurus as the goal?

To this objection—"How is it accepted?"—the response is as follows: O Lord, that which the venerable Ādinātha, who is desired in the primordial seats (*ādiyīthas*) and elsewhere, taught regarding the distinction between the status of the deity and the guru within the reality of the oneness of his own indivisible conscious nature—that has been worshipped and propitiated by all exactly in that manner. (5–7)
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Mahānayaprakāśa composed by the venerable teacher Śitikaṇṭhācārya. || 5 ||

Now begins the sixth chapter. (p. 74) Having thus explained this according to the sequence of the *muṇḍadaṇḍa* of these very Vāmeśīs, he now describes the sequence of worship and transgression according to the northern sequence.

The state of Śiva is the power of the verse; through its manifestation, the wisdom and action of the senses are auspicious. When the essence of consciousness-bliss has arisen, that is the supreme state upon the mountain of the woman who is the embodiment of that [bliss]. || 1 ||

Even regarding the channels, the clusters, the thieves, the directions, the pervasive ones, the boundaries of punishment, the sword, the roots, and the crossroads— therein [he knows] such things as hearing, taste, and the sense of touch.
In the state of the god Bāroṭha, there is the manifestation of the deity; even this [state] is the dissolution of the consciousness of objects. (p.
75) Whether it be intentional or unintentional sin, that too is dissolved within the Bhairava of the senses. 3.
(Tilaka) Previously, the fivefold sequence of vehicles (*pañcavāhakrama*), established through worship, was explained in detail; however,
the internal sequence of the feet (*pātakrama*)— which is devoid of external worship and consists of the movement and circulation of power (*śakti*)— is a secret matter.

Now this is being established: for here, the supreme flow of Śakti, having arisen either successively or simultaneously from the two supports— the Mūlādhāra and the Janmādhāra— is perceived as tending toward a fivefold emergence upon reaching the support of the vital breath (pavana), and upon reaching the vicinity of the Kanda and other centers.

Then, having fallen by its own nature into the fivefold expansion of the rays of touch, it falls atom by atom into the pores of the skin; and by way of residue, the entire host of the splendors born of the senses flashes forth in four ways.
And that expansion of rays, assuming a state of existence as a cluster of channels, abides within the staff of power (*śaktidaṇḍa*).

Falling evenly from the starting point of the eyebrows, it touches the root of the nose; there, at that very place which serves as the gateway for the four sense-faculties and takes the form of a crossroads, it spreads forth.
And from that region, it extends toward the four pairs of gateways known as the eyes, ears, tongue, and nose.
Leaping up and falling down in that sequence, having performed the savoring of external objects,
Bhairava is gratified as He is embraced by the rays of the senses through both the sequential and non-sequential orders of descent. In the *Pātarahasya*,
this very meaning is now applied according to the sequence of word-meanings and sentence-meanings, starting from the word "Śaiva."
The specific rays that arise from the Mūlādhāra, from the Śāktapada, and from the Janmādhāra,

reaching the Pavanādhāra, become manifest; they spread out as tactile sensations from all sides in minute particles within the Kanda and the navel, and thus they are distinguished by their fourfold nature as they first emerge.

"They fall upon the staff of power"— this is the first descent of the four rays of the sense-faculties; thereafter, by the coiling of the cluster of channels (nāḍīs) supported by the staff, having reached the point of impact above, they descend equally to the root of the nose, at the starting place of the two eyebrows, the location of the crossroads.

Having made a second descent with a single flow and entered the two-fold, two-fold situated openings of the sense organs— wherein are the two eyeballs, the two ear-cavities, the two flows of the tongue,
and the two nostrils— one [perceives] the splendors born of the eyes situated in the arrangement of the sensory locations.

The caravan, having descended at the third fall and established itself in its respective domains, completely embraces Bhairava and gratifies him both successively and non-successively; thus, through the immersion into the pair of the fourth and fifth stages, this account is fivefold in its sequence. Indeed, this sequence of falls has been taught by the Lord.
It was taught by way of the *apuṣpa* sequence, and it has been discussed here in this context due to its commonality.
From the station of the Supreme Goddess (*parādevī*) presiding over the supreme ether, the pentad beginning with Vāmeśī is proclaimed;
among these, Vāmeśī resides in the peripheral wheel called Vṛnda, within the fourfold group of Śāmbhavī goddesses, according to the sequence of the five [wheels].
Khecarī shines forth by means of the eight Śākta-siddhas according to the sequence of the first pāda; Bhūcarī by means of the twelve Melāpa-siddhas according to the sequence of the second pāda;
and Saṃhārabhakṣiṇī by means of the sequence of the twenty-four Mantra-siddhas according to the sequence of the third pāda.

Raudreśvarī is [attained] through the sequence of the accomplishment of the sixteen knowledges and through the fifth sequence of the *pāta*; thus is the expanded manifestation of the *pātakrama* divided. 1-2-3.

(p. 78) Now, the nature of the wheel (*cakra*) whose form is the manifestation of bliss (*prakāśānanda*) is revealed by means of a pair of verses: The wheel of the manifestation of the sun is worshipped as the moon of bliss;
it arises from the seven peaks and the ten channels, worshipped as the vital breath of the thread of fire. (4)
In the movement of the emission of the new moon, there is the divine enjoyment consisting of persistence and bliss;
in the ego-sense of the obstruction of conjunction, there is the measure of the object of knowledge. || 5 ||

Because light is distinct from non-light, the manifestation of light is called a "new creation" (*nūtanasṛṣṭi*). At the outset, due to the veneration of its numerical count, it is designated by the name "Light" (*prakāśa*); and through the etymological derivation of that name, it assumes the form of the twelve suns (*dvādaśārka*), thereby possessing the nature of the three abodes (*tridhāma*) within each of the three [cycles]. Thus, the Sun resides in the Wheel of Light (*prakāśacakra*).
It is satisfied and nourished; in this very way, the moon's origin from bliss is a case of metaphorically attributing the cause to the effect.
Thus, in the *ānandacakra*, the sixteen digits (*kalās*) are established as lunar qualities, while in the *mūrticakra*, they are established as fiery qualities.
Prabhā, Mūrti, Prakāśā, Marīci, Tāpanī,
Karālā, and Lelihānā.
Thus, by means of the seven crests (*śikhā*), the ten channels of the arms are joined with the seven crests residing within the mouth;

in this way, the wheel of forms (*mūrticakra*) is seventeenfold. In this manner, the fact that the three sequences consist of the three abodes (*dhāma*) has been internalized and slightly unveiled; and so it is said:

The solar sequence of the abodes (*dhāmakrama*) has the twelve rays as its object; the sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*) consists of the twelve vowels excluding the neuter vowels; those same rays, having first arisen within the twelve unobstructed abodes and fallen into the paths of emptiness, constitute the sequence of consciousness (*saṃvitkrama*). Thus is the pervasion of the wheel of light (*prakāśacakra*).

In the Ānandacakra, there is the sequence of the *dhāman* (abodes) through the expansion of the sixteen channels of the nectar of the *bindu*; the sequence of the *varṇas* (phonemes) through the pervasion of the sixteen vowels together with the neuter vowels; and the sequence of *saṃvit* (consciousness) within the sixteen—the ten faculties of intellect and action, the five breaths, and the mind—such is the pervasion of the Ānandacakra. In the Mūrticakra, [the pervasion occurs] through the channels of the arms...
Through the radiation of seven rays from the face adorned with ten ornaments, the sequence of the abodes (*dhāmakrama*) is seventeenfold.

The sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*), beginning with the letter *a* presided over by the Primordial Phoneme (*ādivarṇa*) and extending up to the letter *ka*, is likewise spread out in seventeen ways. These very lunar stages (*cāndrya bhūmikā*), having turned away from the external, [constitute this sequence].
Even the arrows, though internally mixed with poison, are experienced together with the [sweet] essence; thus, the sequence of consciousness consists of exactly seventeen.

This is the triad of wheels (*cakratraya*) which constitutes the Divine Current (*divyaugha*). Indeed, the entire multitude of objects does not transcend the sequence of abode (*dhāman*), phoneme (*varṇa*), and consciousness (*saṃvit*), because the universe consists of name and form.

The entire multitude of objects included within the universe consists of nothing but name and form; "name" and "form" are interchangeable with "abode" (*dhāman*) and "color" (*varṇa*). Thus, all objects do not abandon their nature of being composed of abode and color.
The universe attains existence by being the support of consciousness; everything that falls within the universe [is thus constituted].
The category of objective entities (*padārthavarga*) remains well-established only when it is entirely supported by consciousness;

thus, it is proven that all phenomena fall within the sequence of the abode (*dhāman*), phoneme (*varṇa*), and consciousness (*saṃvit*). In the first *vāmeśīcakra* of the *Pañcavāha*, all sequences of phonemes, consciousness, and abodes exist without differentiation.

Like the liquid of a peacock’s egg, they remain condensed; then, by way of the sequence of the form of manifest bliss, they are slightly differentiated and unfolded. Indeed, the clear sequence of the multitude of divisions—the Great Sequence of the sequence of phonemes, the sequence of consciousness, the sequence of the lights of the sequence of abodes—is perceived. Thus it is said.

The processes of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal, as well as pervasion, are indicated in this manner within these very wheels (cakras) whose forms are Light, Bliss, and Form—wheels that will have their sentence-meanings established in what follows. One might ask: "How is it that emanation is said to be pervaded by the Sun and maintenance by the Moon, since this appears to be a reversal? For [in reality], emanation belongs to the Moon and maintenance to the Sun."
"Belonging to the Sun"—is this the tradition of the lineage? True;
this account applies to the sequence of arising (*udayakrama*), whereas according to the sequence of dissolution (*vilāpanakrama*), other things are also observed.
Thus, specific interpretations based on different traditions are seen in various places; for instance, fire is indeed illuminated by the light of the sun.
As the Śruti says: "The sun, or Indra, enters Agni at night. Likewise:
"He procreates by means of the pregnant, dual speech.

Thus it is said. Now, is it not the case that the fire-light residing in the bulb (*kanda*) is innate (*sahaja*) within the lineage, whereas the light of the sun and other sources is merely figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), that is, superimposed (*āropita*)? True—yet even that [light], being illumined by the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), attains its existence through that which exists.

[He] obtains [it]; otherwise, however, it would not remain for even a moment. Likewise, for the light of the moon as well, the sun alone is the cause; for *amā* is the name of that ray in which the moon dwells.
Because she dwells in the absence [of the moon], she is therefore remembered as Amāvāsyā.
Likewise,
the rays of the sun falling upon the moon, which consists of water, dispel the darkness of night,
just as rays entering the interior of a mirror dispel the darkness within a chamber.
Thus, regarding the possession of rays by the moon through its replenishment by the sun, Śrī Sāmba says: "Into which the moon— being drunk day after day by gods, ancestors, and men—
enters again and again as it wanes, and from which it increases once more."
I take refuge in that immeasurable nectar of the sun, situated within its orb, in which the Vedas shine like bees hovering over honey.
Thus he praised: "The Sun is the illuminator of both the Moon and Fire, and it is therefore appropriate to mention it first.

In this way, through the terminology of 'illumination' (*prakāśa*), the Sun is the agent of illumination, its nature is light, and it follows after light; whereas reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is lunar, a flowing expansion, the wheel of bliss (*ānandacakra*), and follows after that."
Fire, pervaded by knowledge, will exist in various places within the wheel of forms;

likewise, in the conventional usage of Śiva, Śakti, and the Sun, the Sun is light pervaded by Śiva, and the Moon is reflective awareness (vimarśa) pervaded by Śakti. Thus, in the conventional usage of the natures of Śiva and Vidyā, Śiva is the light, the Sun, and Vidyā—

And Ānanda is the moon. Thus is the sequence of will and knowledge: ultimately, upon the arising of both knowledge and conceptualization, the conceptualization of knowledge—which is already established and synonymous with light—is the lunar outflow that follows in every respect; it is the lunar [light] which, being subsequent, is conjoined with the solar light.
The expansion of bliss: for prāṇa is the sun, apāna is the moon; day is the sun, night is the moon;
piṅgalā is the sun, iḍā is the moon—thus, as previously indicated, it is the sun alone that in every way follows the expansion of the sun, and after its descent, there is the state of nourishment.

For one who has descended and attained stability becomes an agent immediately thereafter; indeed, the action—cast into the third stage, consisting of withdrawal, and situated within the wheel of forms through the pervasion of fire—culminates in itself. Thus, at the outset, the wheel of light alone must be of the nature of emanation. In this manner, the sequence of worship...

All oral traditions, being maintained through an uninterrupted lineage, gain stability exactly as they are established; thus it has been demonstrated that the specific number, the rules of distinction, and the sequence of worship are in every respect unavoidable. || 4 || 5 ||
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Mahānayaprakāśa composed by the venerable teacher Śitikaṇṭhācārya. || 6 ||
Now begins the seventh arising. Now he commences the sequence of Vṛnda: the leader of the wheel of the Śākina-pīṭha, the essence of the lion-throne in the northern quarter.
One should cultivate auspiciousness by bowing with reverence to the teacher of the Bindu-cakra, who is the destroyer of the sense of "mine. 1.

The grammatical construction is: "I bow to the conduct (*ācāra*) of the Vṛndacakras. For conduct, being of the nature of action, is formless; it implies the agent of that conduct, who is substantial in nature. Thus, it results in a salutation to the *śākinīs*. What is this conduct? It is said: first, [the worship] of the Blessed Lady, because of her preeminence.
Having prostrated, the deities situated within the five wheels are then worshipped; this is the *Mahaugha*.

Following that, the worship of the Bhagavatī within the *Siddhaugha*—this is the practice (*ācāra*) which touches upon both systems. Having done what? To this he says: [having worshipped] that very Śrī Maṅgalā, who is the cause for the cessation of the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamatā*).

Having meditated upon her, he distinguishes her as "Śākinī": she is the sole leader within the wheel of the fivefold Śākinīs born of the eight families, presiding as the primary authority over the lion-throne in the Northern House; thus she is praised in her distinctness. Now follows the sequence of the abode, color, and consciousness of this very goddess—the abode and color— [The text continues: ...the abode and color—
For the two sequences (krama), by virtue of the relationship between the signified and the signifier through the movement of word and meaning, consist of the manifestation of name and form;

they are all-pervasive and unavoidable everywhere. And the third sequence, which is consciousness (saṃvit-krama) in the form of the cognizer, is the presiding authority over those two sequences which are of the nature of the object of cognition; without the sequence of consciousness, there would be no sequence of abodes or phonemes.

Even in the state of stability, there are two aspects that appear as non-stable; for, due to their insentience (*jaḍatva*), they are established in every way through the sequence of consciousness (*saṃvit*).

Thus, everywhere, the sequence of the abode (*dhāman*), the phoneme (*varṇa*), and consciousness (*saṃvit*) is both more praiseworthy and unavoidable. And its sequence of consciousness is the creator, the sustainer, the establisher, and the pervasive one.
The reality of the object is complete within this much: the Withdrawer as the place of rest;
the sequence of the Abode belonging to the Goddess Maṅgalā, who is the middle abode consisting of the vibration of Consciousness;

the sequence of phonemes belonging to her, which is the state of being expressed by the five clusters (*piṇḍas*); and consciousness, which is without attributes and the locus of the wheel of Consciousness.

The locus of its establishment is thus the sequence of consciousness (saṃvitkrama); immediately following that is the sequence of the unobscured abode (nirāvaraṇadhāmakrama), which consists of the nature of the supreme space free from obscuration. || 1 ||

Now, the "Great Current" (mahaugha) is the lineage of the Guru (gurukrama), and that is indeed the lineage of Vṛnda (vṛndakrama), which has been taught in detail in the *Kramasadbhāva*; here it is presented by way of extension through the traditional succession of teachings as they have come down:
"From the five-fold [lineage] of Muduvalita, transmitted through the left-hand path of the assembly, the movement of Vṛndinī and Īśī."
The sequence of the fierce lord who has achieved knowledge, the one who possesses hands, is undivided and of the nature of compassion. 2.
"Enveloped by the five mudrās—enumerate them," meaning "count them. How so? He says:
Jñānasiddhā is Raudreśvarī and Karaṅkiṇī; Mantrasiddhā is Grāsakī and Krodhanī; Melāpasiddhā is Bhūcarī and Bhairavī; Śāktasiddhā is Khecarī and Lelihānā.
The Śāmbhava-siddhā is Vāmeśvarī, the Khecarīmudrā; such is the enumeration according to the sequence.

She who causes the body composed of the five elements to rest in the supreme space is Karaṅkiṇī—this is the mudrā of the Jñāna-siddhas. She who [rests] in the mantra-body consisting of twenty-four principles...
"She who embraces [all] is Krodhanī"—this is the mudrā of the Mantra-siddhas. "She who always moves in the voids (kha) is Khecarī"—this is the mudrā of the Śāmbhava-siddhas. || 2 ||
The sixteen vowels are the mantra-skin; they are joined with the consonants.
The eight vowels beginning with *a* are the Śambhu-kula, while the goddesses of the letters (*gāsadevī*) and the goddesses of the syllables (*cauradevī*) do not form a group. (3)
This is the enumerative statement for the five divisions of the Vṛndadevīs;

thus, by means of the two [verses] "the pentad of mudrās" (*pañcamudrā*) and "the sixteen ñānarāvas," the structural framework (*pīṭhikābandha*) of the Śākinī-cakra is established. Herein is the sequential index: "Mṛtakā" and "Ñānarūpā."
By two [terms], there is the instruction on the nature of the *jñānasiddha*; by one, "binduśirī," there is the instruction on the nature of the *mantrasiddha*;
by the three—*hrasvadīrgha*, *pariṇamana*, and *akucita*—there is the instruction on the nature of the *melāpasiddha*;
and by "sattama," "aṣṭama," "akyāpīṭha," and "kulapadmā" [there is the instruction on the nature of the *kulasiddha*].

Thus, with the five [terms] *candāne*, *iti*, *amaka*, *la*, and *iti*, there is the instruction on the nature of the Śākta-Siddha; with the two [terms] *assaru* and *ñānakriyā*, there is the instruction on the nature of the Śāmbhava-Siddha; and with the four [terms] *vāmeśyu*, *aṣṭapīṭha*, *ādivanna*, and *mātṛka*, there is the determination of the nature of the Vṛnda. Thus [it is said].
Seventeen; together with the three preceding ones, the meaning of the sentences amounts to twenty. || 3 ||
He joins this very [teaching] with distinct sentence-meanings:
"The sun of the impurity of death and birth, O Rāvu, rises at every moment; O Nañā, give it to me! (p.
89) At every moment the sun rises in the sky; O Goddess, give that sixteen-fold [essence] to me. (4)

Regarding *mṛtaka* and *sūtaka*: elsewhere these refer to Śiva and Śakti, or to the prāṇa and apāna; [they also refer to] the emergence and entry of Śakti, the paths of Piṅgalā and Iḍā, and Nāda and Bindu as short and long [vowels]. Here, however, *sūtaka* refers to the protracted (*pluta*) vowel, while *miśra* refers to the long [vowel]; thus, there are five short sounds for the *mṛtakas* and five long sounds for the *miśras*.

With the five *sūtaka* sounds, which are prolonged cries—thus, with fifteen cries, the sixteenth is the *muṇḍarāva*. That sixteenth [sound] is the very first phoneme that touches the two limits (*koṭi*) in order to dissolve the lunar digits (*kalā*) one by one; thus, the emergence of the sixteenfold cry is the path of knowledge (*jñānamārga*).

And although their rising clamor subsides moment by moment, it becomes ever-new through their innate passion and the pride of their Śākta power, just like the ringing of the bells of the goddesses of sound. || 4 ||
He says that very thing:
"The nature of knowledge is the support; let it resound with power as far as the highest peak. (p.
90) "Three, five, [and so on]—let it be until non-existence; in the absence of [anything], the offering is the completely fulfilled emptiness. || 5 ||
This support, which has the form of the head, is composed entirely of knowledge through its power— that is, through its own specific radiance,

through knowledge born of the other [external] sense organs, as well as through the supreme *bindu*, and through that which is even further beyond, residing in the aperture of the skull; thus, the support is threefold and consists solely of knowledge, as the scripture states:
"He beholds the supreme state through the aperture at the crown of the head.
Likewise,
"the yogi situated within the *bindu* always knows everything."
Thus: and there is another [knowledge] born of the senses, accessible to all. In that threefold knowledge, the very first phoneme alone remains undivided;

it unfolds as the sixteen vowels by its innate nature, and through the state of being a seed produced from the differentiation of tones, it becomes pervasive. In the extraction consisting of sixteen parts, that very same [phoneme] undergoes manifestation; it is that very same one.
When there is the state of the sixteenfold [constituent], consisting of the intellect, the organs of action, the objects of the senses, and the mind,

having become full with that same number of lunar digits (*kalā*), one becomes an offering in the seventeenfold abode— which is free from the conceptualization of the single digit and devoid of limiting adjuncts— and attains complete integration (*sāmarasya*) in all its limbs. || 5 ||
Now, regarding the nature of one perfected in mantra: one should contemplate the reality of the mantra as adorned with the *bindu* at its head, extending through the aperture of the skull;
from the opening of the mouth, the king of mantras and so forth should be uttered within the triad of the *puryaṣṭaka*.

To dispel the doubt as to how the letters from *ka* to *bha*—numbering twenty-four—can attain the status of mantra, the traditional teaching (*saṃpradāya*) states: when they are adorned by the nasal drop (*bindu*) through its placement upon the head, they are then addressed as mantras; thus, the matrices (*yonis*) beginning with *ka* and ending with *bha*, together with the *bindu*, [are recited] by way of the upward breath (*udāna*).

The attainment of the status of mantra occurs through their being uttered; by those very mantras, the enumeration of the principles (tattvas) from earth up to primordial nature (prakṛti) is inferred. Therefore, it is established that these Śākinīs consist of exactly twenty-four impure principles. This inference is the establishment of the principles, and they—

Even when the sound of the staff (*daṇḍarāva*) manifests, it is manifested only within the cavity of the mouth; thus, the sound of the staff also results ultimately in the sound of the skull (*muṇḍarāva*). For, according to the mantra-adepts, it is only upon the subsiding of the sound that there is the subsiding of even the three *puryaṣṭakas*. (p. 92) 6.
Now, regarding the accomplished *melāpas*:

the short and long vowels, the consonants (*hal*), and the semi-vowels (*aj*); the *sañjī* and *pakiti* [groups] beginning with *i* and *y*; in the twelve *melās*, the *mātrīs*, the *rañjīs*, the *yonibījas*, and the *assaras*. (7)

Through three sentences, including the two that will be spoken hereafter, the fusion (*melāpa*) of the perfected ones of the fusion is twelvefold; therein, when the phonemes of the *mātṛkā* arise in a single sequential order,
there is a fusion consisting of eight types of euphonic combination (*sandhi*), as well as a fourfold fusion consisting of the abodes of consciousness (*saṃvid-dhāma*).

For example—the union (*melāpa*) of the short and the long is the Auspicious Abode (*śivāyatana*), which is the very designation of the long form; and the closest proximity (*paraḥ sannikarṣaḥ*) of consonants (*halām*) and vowels (*acām*) is the *saṃhitā*, which is the union in the form of euphonic combination (*sandhi*). "This is the Blessed One, this is the Blessed One" is the second [type of union]; it is the conjunction of preceding and following consonants alone.

"Bhagavān jagatprabhuḥ" (The Blessed One, Lord of the World)—this is the third [case], known as *halasañjñī* (the designation of a consonant). Now, regarding *pakiti*: this is the state of *prakṛtibhāva* (naturalness), where even though not changed, it is treated as changed; it consists of the natural state of two vowels, as in "a apīhi" and "i indraṃ paśya"—this is the fourth.

The euphonic combination (*sandhi*) characterized by the relationship between the original element (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*), according to the rule *iko yaṇ aci*, occurs when the vowels *i* and so forth— which constitute the original forms— are replaced by the consonants *ya* and so forth, as in the example *paśyāmy atra* and others; and here,
the four vowels beginning with *i* manifest in the form of semivowels (*antasthā*) during the euphonic combination, and furthermore—
The fifth [type of] transformation (*pariṇāma*) is that which exists in the state of the *pada*, wherein they abide in their original form; this is the "excellent" (*prakṛṣṭa*) transformation.

Furthermore, there is another [transformation], which consists of the conjunction and disjunction of different vowels from a single source such as the letter *ka*—namely, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the twelve mothers excluding the neutral vowels (*ṣaṇḍhasvara*), such as *ka*, *kā*, *ki*, *kī*, and so forth—and likewise:

The sixth is the *melāpa* (conjunction) consisting of a *sandhi-saṃyoga* (conjunctive union), which occurs through the pervasion of twelve *mātrās* that have become doubled, belonging to the twelve *yoni*-letters starting with *ka*— namely *kra, kna, kma, kva, kya, kla, kta, ksa, kca, kpa, ktra*, and ending with *kṣa*— just as described previously.

Likewise, by means of the vowel-less letter *a*, there is the internal empowerment (*antaradhiṣṭhāna*) and all-pervasive nature of the forty-nine [phonemes]— namely, the fifteen seed-syllables ending with *aḥ*, and the thirty-four matrices (*yoni*) beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*— through their state of being contained within one another, such as *ka* and *kha*.

The seventh [melāpa] consists of the utterance of the Mātṛkā beginning with *ga*, *gha*, *ṅa*, and so forth; it is dependent on the vowels of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) together with their matrices (*sayoni*).
Now, he describes the *melāpa* consisting of *saṃprasāraṇa*, characterized by the relationship between the original base (*sthānin*) and its substitute (*ādeśa*), as follows:
"In the state of transformation, when there is the substitution of *i* for *da* and others, the original base is produced by the subsequent [element]."
In the absence of the manifestation of the six sense-bases, this great element is in a state of complete dissolution.
The four semivowels (*antaḥstha*), beginning with *ya*, undergo a transformation into the form of the four vowels beginning with *i*;

and this transformation of the substituends (*sthānin*) into the form of the substitutes (*ādeśa*) is "excellent" (*prakṛṣṭa*), because there is no return to their original form. In this same way, the powers (*śakti*) beginning with *ya* [reside] in Śiva in the form of *i* and the others.

The matrices (*yonayaḥ*) and phonemes (*vyañjanāni*) transform into the state of seeds during the stage of *saṃprasāraṇa*; thus, the four great elements evolve. This is just as [the substitution] "ijyā" is grasped when it is said "ukta," and so forth, because it has been defined by the rule: "The *ig* and *yaṇ* [substitutes] are *saṃprasāraṇa*" (Pāṇini 1.1.45). Thus ends the eighth meeting (*melāpa*). || 8 ||
Now, through the sequence of the abode of consciousness, there is a union (*melāpa*):
in the state where there is no unevenness and no lack of aesthetic equilibrium (*asāmarasya*), there is a union of the two vehicles of the couple.
In the uneven discourse of the husband and wife, the twelve knots (*dvādaśagranthi*) are dissolved by one who is unskilled [in worldly ways].

First, there is the natural and all-pervasive state of the equilibrium between Śiva and Śakti, consisting of the nature of Light (prakāśa) and Reflexive Awareness (vimarśa); that too is "without parts" (akalāpa)— that is, when everything has subsided— and yet,
by means of those parts of this primordial syllable which, by their very fitness, are unobstructed and partless (niṣkalā), it is the supreme moment.

The state of being free from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇībhāva*) alone is the first [point] that must always be kept in mind; when that exists, there is a second, the "Great Withdrawal" (*mahāsaṃhāra*), characterized by the simultaneous entry of the twelve rays into the thirteenth;
and third, the merging with each respective object individually through the process of becoming one with it (*tanmayībhāva*).

It occurs in three ways according to the sequence of consciousness; furthermore, there is a fourth way, arising from the central path (*madhyamārga*) through the churning of the fire and wind of power (*śakti*), together with the twelve knots consisting of the forms of the powers known as Māyā, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, Sadāśiva, Indhikā, Dīpikā, Baidava, Nāda, and the rest.
The twelfth [chapter] is the *melāpa* (conjunction) according to the sequence of abodes (*dhāma*) enumerated by the divisions of touch (*sparśabheda*).

Thus, the *melāpa* is the nature of the collection (*samavāya*) of the universe, which consists of the consciousness of phonemes (*varṇasaṃvit*) and whose essence is the conjunction of Śiva and Śakti; this is the instruction on the true nature of one perfected through *melāpa*. || 9 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Mahānayaprakāśa* composed by the venerable teacher Śitikaṇṭha. 7.
Now begins the eighth chapter. Next, he describes the nature of the Śākta-siddhas in five verses:
Sattama, Aṣṭama, Vaggyu, Yājī, Śājī, Cauraghoṣa, and Mahāghoṣa.
The goddess Śātā, who frequents assemblies for worship, nourishes the body like a well-composed verse. || 1 ||

The letters ending in *a* have been previously assigned as the radiant [manifestations]. And the letter *ma*, by virtue of its nature as a contact consonant (*sparśa*), is an internal factor that assists through conjunction. Thus, in the state of each [letter] becoming the form of *ra*, it is applied at the end in the form of a *bindu*, because it belongs to the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Due to the disappearance of the form that serves as the seed-syllable (*bīja*), the vowel-less letter *ma* is called the *anusvāra*; such is the prior account. Furthermore, the letters from *ya* onwards are described as being limbs of the *melāpa*, existing in the nature of both transformation and non-transformation; the three letters beginning with *śa* are unvoiced (*aghoṣa*), while the letter *ha* is the great voiced (*mahāghoṣa*). Thus, these [are established].
The two groups beginning with *ya* and *śa* are pervaded by the goddesses who are their Śaktis;

thus, through the worship of these phonemes, the abode of Śakti (*śāktadhāma*) is attained. Furthermore, the letter *kṣa*, being the phoneme of withdrawal (*saṃhāravarṇa*), does not desire to nourish other phonemes because it is inherently composed of four parts—this is the view of the Śākta-siddhas.
The sequence of the syllables. || 1 ||
Now, the sequence of their abodes:
she rests within the body of the Aṣṭirūpī, who has emerged from the Śākini of the Akya-pīṭha. (p.
98) She dwells everywhere in all the various places, above, below, and in the intermediate directions. || 2 ||
The lineage of the family is radiant with the stalks of the lotus; it flows with the waters of the ocean and is perfected by the footprints of the sages.
It is adorned with the excellent conduct of those who remember the truth, and it is enriched by the downward-flowing streams of the drops of nectar.
(A pair of verses:
The Śākinī born from a single seat is the eighth, having attained the number of the most excellent through her forms;
she causes rest in the positions practiced above and below, and those positions are eight because—

Flowing upward from the source of birth— the region of the fire at the *kanda*— and from the lotus of the navel, [the breath] comes to rest at its conclusion within the threshold of the heart; likewise, its state of abiding between the mouth and the palate consists of a repose through the cessation of upward and downward movement, by means of the internal upward and downward expansion of these three.
Having established the state of the *bindu*-cakra and the upper cakra, that arising which occurs through the process of enveloping is enriched by the downward movement;
it bestows prosperity through the downward movement—that is, by entering the *kula* and thereby nourishing it—due to resting in the supreme station (*parāsthāna*). || 2 ||
Having explained the meaning, he analyzes it further: "In the drinking of the juice of the *lampikā* flower, the drop (*bindu*) rests in the expansion of the *aṇḍa*.
In the measuring of the digestive power (*pācaka-śakti*) at the navel, the seminal fluid (*reta*) resides in the cavity of the drop. (3)

When there is stability in the *bindu*, then one attains the drinking of the essence of the moon situated above—this is the remainder [of the sense]. This is the lunar radiance of the abode (*dhāmaprakāśa*). And by the expansion of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), find rest;
this is the extraordinary, solar radiance of the abode, specifically that of the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) in the navel.

The state of being the cooker belongs to the heat (*ūṣman*); for even though it pervades the entire body, the "forcible digestion" (*haṭhapāka*) occurs only in the gastric fire—this is the external [view]. Thus, the sequence of the three abodes is the dissolution of all the lunar digits (*bindu-kalā*) within the *kanda*; this has been described by means of the property of the new moon (*āmāvasya*), and thus is the sequence of the abode of residence. || 3 ||
He describes the sequence of consciousness: following the stainless digit of the new moon (*amākalā*), one should enter the path of the bridge (*setubandha*) by means of the Supreme (*parā*) state.
By means of the upward-rising lunar flow, the Goddess of the Kula remains tranquil. (4)
Arising from the point (bindu) or from the surface of the door-panel, and entering by way of the bridge situated at the rear,

there is rest in the station of Parā; thus, all eight [energies] that have arisen pervade with their final, nectar-like digit the life-force of the entire aggregate of the Kula belonging to one established in the expansion of Vyāna— this is the meaning.

For the Śāktas, there is the sequence of consciousness (*saṃvitkrama*), because through all eight risings it is the moon alone that undergoes liquefaction; and this culminates in the supreme bliss and aesthetic wonder of the Self, which is the *kulapiṇḍa* beyond [the moon].
This is the essential nature of the Śākta Siddha. || 4 ||
Then the Śāmbhava-siddhas:
*assarujanabhedya-rañjīji raudra-vāma-jeṭhyu-ambeta*. (p.
101) Having joined the final letter of *cākalu* [with the first], it becomes the *śāmbhava-paśama-daśā-khaṃbhetta*. 5.
Just as the vowel *a* is divided into four parts by means of its divisions of *kalās*, so too the final letter *kṣa*—
the syllable of reabsorption (*saṃhārārṇa*) consisting of four *kalās*— is divided into the letters *ka*, *ṣa*, *a*, and the *visarga*.

How so? He says: "Having stilled the Śāmbhavī states of tranquility, having rent them asunder, and having caused [the consciousness] to enter within"—this is the sequence of phonemes for the Śāmbhava-siddhas. || 5 ||
Now, the sequence of consciousness (*saṃvitkrama*): It dissolves the rays of knowledge and action; it is swallowed by the power of Śiva’s grace.
It is the devourer of the essence of bliss; it is swallowed by the perfected state of the *aiśvara* [level] which bestows awakening. 6.

It is characterized by the force of the plural number as "the dissolver of all twelve expansions of knowledge and action simultaneously in a single moment," for the dissolution of each individual function occurs one by one.

(p. 102) "Always for all people" is not a limb of yoga; this is a statement made after having gathered [the various points] together through dissolution (*vilāpa*). This is because of the dissolution of external objects, as well as the non-conceptualization (*akalpana*) of Śiva, Śakti, and the Self, of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, and of the Self along with its conceptualizations and the objects of those conceptualizations, within the state that is beyond breath (*aprāṇabhūmi*).

Due to their setting (pratyastamaya), there is likewise the dissolution of supreme bliss and reflective awareness (vimarśa) into the ground consisting solely of pure consciousness; this is the meaning. Furthermore, at the conclusion, in the fourth stage, even supreme consciousness itself is swallowed. By means of these four "bites," the Śāmbhava Siddhas are of four kinds.

They become partakers of accomplishment; thus, their sequence is that of consciousness (*saṃvitkrama*), and their entry is the sequence of the abodes (*dhāmakrama*), which is the essential nature of the *Śāmbhava-siddhas*. Likewise, when one whose eyes have been suddenly opened possesses the knowledge of observation regarding the object of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), that is the knowledge of the *Jñāna-siddhas*, [perceiving] "this is thus" and "not thus."
The reflective awareness that "it is not thus, but rather it is thus" is itself the *mantra* for those perfected in *mantra*;

the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between the object of knowledge and the knower is the *melāpa* (conjunction) for those perfected in *melāpa*; and the Śākta-krama is the means of attaining that abode of consciousness wherein the division of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge dissolves.

The repose of the Śāktasiddhas also sets in the supreme abode; that is the abode of the Śāmbhavasiddhas. Furthermore, those who possess the perfection of knowledge reach the ultimate limit of divine knowledge, and those who possess the perfection of mantra reach the ultimate limit of mantra-perfection.

And those who possess the accomplishment of *melāpa* [attain it] through reaching the ultimate limit by resting in the fruit of *melāpa*; those who are accomplished in Śakti [attain it] at the stage of having reached the ultimate limit by relying on the final stage of the arising of Śakti; and those who are accomplished in Śambhu [attain it likewise].

By means of touching the stages culminating in the practice of taking food only until one is satisfied, they attain, within a single abode, simultaneously and at one and the same time, the unsurpassed state of rest alone. || 6 ||
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Mahānayaprakāśa* composed by the venerable teacher Śitikaṇṭhācārya. || 8 ||
Now begins the ninth chapter.

Next, in order to remove the misconception that the deity of the letter *ma* is the sixty-fifth, he says: "O Mistress of the Left, in the five-streamed quality, the enjoyment of the root is for the sake of creation."
104) By means of the five auspicious signs and the eight qualities of the Kameṇa [tree], she purifies the flood of those who are to be worshipped. || 1 ||

It has been stated that the twelve functions (*vṛtti*), presided over by the five Vāmeśvarīs in their respective divisions, become sixty; when combined with the four [functions] beginning with *sṛṣṭi* born from the Root (Mūla), they become sixty-four. Thus, how can the Goddess of the letter *Ma* be the sixty-fifth among them?
For she, having crossed the great flood and being liberated, is worshipped within the assembly of the Siddhas. || 1 ||
Right here he states another alternative:

"In the eight seats, in the eight-fold [tradition], in the eight-times-eight, and in the eight great currents; in the five times eight-fold lineage of Kameśvara, from the beginning to the end, is the Siddhaugha of the Leader. (2)
From each of the eight seats (*pīṭha*), there are eight *śākinīs*, thus they total exactly sixty-four; nevertheless, how does the goddess Makāra become the sixty-fifth? For she...

(p. 105) Even though she has reached the beginning and the end of the *śākinī*-circle, she is worshipped as one and the same within the distinct multitude of *siddhas*; and that there is a pervasion by the letter *ma* for her—this is incorrect, because the letter *ma* is established in the twenty-fifth stage.

It has already been largely explained how one who possesses thirty-three consonants pursues the goddess Makāra; however, since it remains to be stated according to the sequence of the *Vṛnda* by means of the numerical correspondence of the sequence of phonemes, he expresses that in another way through a pair of verses:
The fifteen powers of Śiva are of five types: short, long, prolated, and ultra-prolated (u).
The eight diphthongs are likewise joined with the nasal bindu in the eight petals of the lotus. || 3 ||
The eight syllables, accompanied by three [short vowels] in the *akka-bīha-kā* positions, constitute the *paribhāva* [meter]. (p.
106) In the *palaya-vanna-ja* [meter], there are five *dṛṣṭa* syllables, followed by two *maru* and one *bhūmi*. || 4 ||
(Yugalaka) The first letter alone is extended everywhere; through the pervasion of Śiva it consists of the five short vowels,
through the pervasion of Śakti the five long vowels, and by means of the prolated vowels— thus there are fifteen vowels, as follows:

The four diphthongs (sandhyakṣara), being eternally long, become eight through the distinction between long and protracted [vowels]; likewise, there are four with the *yamakas*—namely *kuṃ*, *khuṃ*, *guṃ*, and *ghuṃ*—and four with the *anusvāra*, *visarjanīya*, *jihvāmūlīya*, and *upadhmānīya*. Thus [there are sixteen].

With the eight primary supports—thus there are thirty-one belonging to the class of vowels; likewise, the five groups of the Mātṛkā are multiplied by five, and the *ya* and *śa* groups are multiplied by four—making thirty-three; on both sides this totals sixty-four, and thus, having transcended these, the sixty-fifth is the letter of dissolution (*pralayavarṇa*).

The letter *kṣa* is the ocean of withdrawal (*saṃhārārṇa*). Having entered that state which is the desert-land (*marubhūmi*)—which is inexpressible (*anuccārya*), nameless (*anākhyā*), in which the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge have dissolved, and which is accessible through the experience of pure existence alone—this is the pervasion of the letters as stated for each step in the Vṛndakrama. Thus ends [the section on] the Vṛndakrama.
The great flood. || 3 || 4 ||
(p. 107) Now he speaks of the streams of Siddhas, Mānavas, and Śiṣyas:
"Hara, Śira, Jina, Gaṅgī, Avatāra, Na, Tā, Jā, Nu, Maṅgala, Pīṭha, Diśāna—this is the stream of Mānavas.
Tristhāna, Kulāra, Na, Bhānupāda, and the eight disciples. (5)

Śrī Maṅgalā alone is the vessel for the descent [of power] into the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and the directions; just as she is the celestial river on the head of Hara, and she, in the form of the multitude of Siddhas, is the queen of the eyes of the multitude of humans known as Hrasvanātha—
she is the fire-drill (araṇi) for the Kula, that is, the source of the specific lineage (ovallī), like the fire-drill for the three fires.

This is the place of origin; and from there, at the end of the lineage of Manu, came Bhānupāda, the foremost of the stream of disciples and the lord of eight disciples, from among whom Queen Īśānā received the source of the tradition. || 5 ||
He introduces that very point:
"The Great One (Mahat), who is like the rising sun, pervades all the world-protectors (Prajāpatis);
the dawn-like radiance of that [Great One] pervades the circle of the quarters, just as the sun [pervades] the opening young lotuses. (p. 108)

Just as Mahādeva is the manifester of the eight forms, or Brahmā of those many Prajāpatis, or the dawn of the rising sun of that vast circle of directions, even so is Bhānu— the Śrīcakrabhānu— the manifester of the lotuses of his disciples. Thus [ends verse 6].
In this very sequence of succession, he praises the lineage of gurus:
"May the unchanging lineage of gurus, like a row of lamps in a succession of lineages, dispel the darkness for people; may its blazing splendor arise incessantly and protect the quarters. (7)

Such a lineage of *ovallis* is seen to have arisen; it is the path of means (*upāya*) free from modification, shining like a row of lamps in the darkness, illuminating both itself and others—thus [are] the *siddhaugha*, *mānavaugha*, and *śiṣyaugha*. || 7 ||
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Mahānayaprakāśa composed by the venerable teacher Śitikaṇṭha. 9.
Now begins the tenth chapter. (p. 109) Now follows the introduction to the Mahākrama;
for the sake of entering [the practice], there is the worship of the Mahākrama and the homage to the Guru.
Thus, having fallen from the pledge, there is likewise an indication for the sake of avoiding the attainment of kingship. || 1 ||

This has been taught as having attained the status of being an accessory (*parikara*) to the Great Sequence (*mahākrama*); now, its indication as falling within the conventional order (*samaya*) is reached, just as the perception of a king arises from observing his retinue. || 1 ||
Now, he describes the definition [of the process] through the mutual vitalization of the speaker, the spoken, and the transition:
"O Speaker! The transition between the signifier and the signified, which is the movement within the intermediate direction, is proclaimed.
The transition of the speaker, the act of worship, and the transition itself—the movement that is the state of being, the color, and the abode—is consciousness. (2)

(p. 110) Although the cognitions of word, meaning, and consciousness flash forth as terminating within the wall of the Supreme Consciousness (*paracit*), each pair among them establishes its own locus through an internal manifestation; thus, all three, though possessing a triple nature, manifest according to their own essential form, just as speaking, worshiping, and transmitting [the teaching] proceed by means of such respective functions.
Through their arrangement, they appear as if mutually vitalized; thus,

one must contemplate how the description, worship, and transmission of phonemes (varṇa), abodes (dhāman), and consciousness (saṃvit) are entirely interpenetrated by one another, for that single reality of the object is presented in a threefold manner.
Now he states the summary of the sequence of the wheel (*cakrakrama*):

"By means of the sudden manifestation of the treasury of unbroken awakening—through the spontaneous arising of *akasmika-karma*—and by the power of worshipping within and without the arrangement of *Kula* and *Kaula*, [the goal is attained]. (3)

By means of the wish-fulfilling gem of consciousness, whose nature is non-sequential and indivisible, and which— without any deliberate mental effort or synthesis within itself— spontaneously manifests the specific stages that are non-different from its own essence;
thereafter, by the power of the supreme speech (*parāvāk*) upon the stage of the lineage (*kulabhūmi*).
(p. 111) By means of the sequence of the wheels (*cakra*) beginning from the channel-wheel (*nāḍicakra*) located at the aperture of the birth-place and ending with the wheel of peace (*śāntacakra*),
in both ways— that Supreme Lord who has been manifested after being experienced within the Divine Current (*divyaugha*)—
having entered the body of Ādinātha, is [to be worshipped] externally on the plane of Kula and Kaula precisely by means of the sequence of the wheels as the object of worship.

Thus, in all the Kula traditions, that very internal arising which exists through the sequence of Śakti is indeed [attained] by means of the specific experiences of their respective stages (*bhūmikā*),

by those who have assumed the form of the *cakracarīs* and are worshipped in their specific configurations, and also by the process of conduct (*caryākrama*) for the sake of unfolding one's own essential nature.
The meaning of the sequence should be cultivated; and thus says the scripture:
"In whichever excellent wheel there is the bliss of satisfaction from its touch, that yoga which consists of supporting it is prescribed as worship itself."
This is the intention of those previously established, according to this underlying purpose. || 3 ||
Then he speaks of the Great Sequence (*mahākrama*):
"One should enter the five supreme wombs, beginning with Will (*icchā*) and so forth, and beginning with Emanation (*sisṭi*) and so forth. (p.
112) Emanation (*sisṭi*), the Equal Flavor (*samarasa*), Vanyu, Icchā, and Kamu—these are manifested as the descent of the deity. || 4 ||

The powers beginning with Will (*icchā*) and those beginning with Emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) are themselves the five supreme matrices (*yonis*). Having plunged into and entered the other expansions of emanation, and having brought about an incarnation through the six phonemes, they consume the sequence; for from that [sequence] arise the five powers of the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) in due order.

Presided over by that many rays of light, they bring the process of emanation to completion; for this primordial Goddess, the supreme power of consciousness (*parā saṃvit*), attaining density through the swelling forth of bliss and consciousness and so on, assumes the form of the *yoni* (womb) and, by manifesting the evolution of the great elements, arranges the expansion of the universe and the course of worldly existence.

These expansions of emanation, numbering twenty-five in form and divided fivefold, consist of the nature of phonemes (*varṇa*), abodes (*dhāman*), and consciousness (*saṃvit*); at the time of worship, they do not transcend the rule of the sixfold phonemes.
Thus, within the expansion of emanation characterized by the sixfold phonemes, the meaning of the sequence [is realized] through the immersion into the stages of descent.

It is manifested fivefold; indeed, the radiance of the *praṇava* in the form of the fivefold whirlpool within the *kuṇḍalinī* exists through its pervasion of the fivefold universe by means of the blossoming of the pentad consisting of the *kanda*, the navel, the heart, the mouth, and the center of the eyebrows.

And although the sequence of the abode (*dhāmakrama*), which consists of the first vibration, is the source for all consonants without distinction, it is primarily the fivefold source beginning with the *ka*-group and ending with the *pa*-group that exists within both *paśyantī* and *madhyamā*, as well as in *ghoṣaṇī*.
The nature of sound (*ghoṣasvabhāvatā*) is that which is manifested at the prior limit of *vaikharī* speech; as they say:
"The sound (*nāda*), originating from space and air, emerging from the body, reaches the mouth;
being differentiated in various places of articulation, it attains the state of phonemes (*varṇa*), and that is what is called 'speech' (*śabda*)."

Thus, it arises as sound; together with that which is to be sounded (*ghoṣaṇī*), that single [sound] becomes twofold, and through this fourfold nature of these utterances, the fivefold emergence— which occurs by means of the supreme speech (*parāvāk*) presiding over the quartet of speech— is itself the sequence of phonemes, the expansion of consciousness through the expansion of the pentad of the senses beginning with hearing.

Likewise, there is the sequence of consciousness through the expansion of the five causes beginning with Brahmā, and the sequence of objects through the sequence of the five [objects] beginning with sound; thus, this entire sequence is the sequence of the abode of consciousness. And the pervasion of the supreme consciousness by all these is proclaimed as non-dual.
Thus, this fivefold womb, which serves as the instrument [of manifestation], should be understood as being of this nature; such is the sequence of emanation. || 4 ||
Now he describes the sequence of abiding:
"The fourth state, deep sleep, and waking—these the perfected one of knowledge abandons as formless.
Stealing, departing, and knowing the ocean—he is the pervasive one, whose form is the dissolution of all things. (5)

Through the pervasion of the four states beginning with the Fourth (turya), the four Siddhas of Knowledge are worshipped by means of the mantras of the four castes; the sequence of the abodes (dhāmakrama) of the four Siddhas of Knowledge corresponds to the four stages beginning with the Fourth,
just as the sequence of phonemes (varṇakrama) corresponds to the presiding of the four groups of vowels, like the fluid within a peacock's egg.
That supreme space which has sprouted forth by becoming the womb of the universe is the first *jñānasiddha*;

that which is the arising of the first vibration is the second *jñānasiddha*; and the consciousness situated amidst the senses, free from modification, is the third *jñānasiddha*—[this being] of the mental states extended toward the external.

(p. 115) The inward-turned reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which effects a state of aesthetic-mystical equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) within the self through reversion, is the fourth, the perfected one of knowledge (*jñānasiddha*). This is the sequence of consciousness (*saṃvitkrama*) of the perfected ones (*siddhas*). For these [deities] are the presiding lords over touch, form, taste, and fragrance, having respectively become solidified.

Although they are necessarily involved in the manifestation of air, fire, water, and earth— excluding the formless elemental ether and likewise the abode beyond the fourth (turyātīta)— those whose power of absolute freedom is complete nevertheless set in motion and sustain the course of worldly existence, even though they are not so involved. As for he who...

In the lineage of the *pīṭhas*, a variation in the manuscript tradition is observed extending up to the son of the King of the *dūtīs*; however, this does not in any way achieve consistency, for it must be that any external object, whatever it may be, must possess a name, form, and designation. Thus it is said.

Four Siddhas are designated by the names Śrīkhagendra, Kūrma, Meṣa, and Macchanda. Elsewhere, in another system of philosophy, these same four— Khagendra and the others— are referred to by those very names according to the sequence of the Kulākulakrama, following its specific Kulākulic methodology.

"Those who have attained association with the daughter of the king through their connection with her messenger are here established as objects of worship"—this is a sinful mode of expression. How indeed can a mere commonality of name be the cause of non-difference?
For example, [one might say] "Rāma, the son of Daśaratha," or "Rāmadeva, the son of the eminent sage Vāmadeva," or "Bhārgava."

Or, O Rāma, since they are designated as one through their unity, the former teachers— who are deceived by this identity of name and who fall into error elsewhere due to such similarity of names— should not be followed; for the Goddess Parā Consciousness is fourfold.
Since she is the cause for the manifestation of the entire cosmic expansion through the specific stages of creation, maintenance, withdrawal, and the ineffable (anākhyā),
