and is worshipped externally by means of the fourfold sequence precisely for the sake of becoming one with her,
what room is there for the worship of a junior lineage of gurus? Thus, [the worship] is by means of the four alone.

The sequence of maintenance (sthitikrama) is accomplished by those perfected in knowledge (jñānasiddha). Now, one might ask: "Are not the twelve daughters of the King [the months] suitable to be members of the sequence of maintenance through their pervasion of the sequence of the rays of knowledge and action?
True—but since the rays will be specified in the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama), what is the point [of mentioning them here]?

[This would involve] redundancy. Now, if it is argued that since dissolution is logically preceded by persistence, it is better to indicate the sequence of the *marīci* [levels] within the sequence of persistence, we say: no, for the waking state consists of the sequence of the *marīci* levels, provided one avoids the notion of a mere linear flow (*vāha*) regarding the waking state. (p. 117)
Since no intrinsic nature whatsoever is possible, it is established that in the process of persistence, the expansion of rays arises spontaneously;
thus, it is not fit to be designated as separate. Therefore, the fourfold non-existence alone is superior. || 5 ||

Now he describes the sequence of withdrawal: "O Jñānaśakti, shine! O Upasa, O Ṣaḍvidha, O Añña, O Kriyāmayīśakti! O Rudravatī, destroy the intellect! O Khasā, [be present] in all conduct; this is the essence of the compendium. (6)

That very power, having emanated in six ways through the divisions of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), is likewise seen in six forms as the empirical power of action (*kriyāśakti*); from among these, she who abides in the state of non-discursive reflection (*nirvicārā*) has, by the destruction of the intellect, adorned herself with the number eleven by breaking [the previous count].
This very sequence of abodes (dhāmakrama) attains the form of a mantra consisting of eleven phonemes:

beginning with the letter *ya* and ending with the letter *ha*, it comprises eight in number; thereafter, through the initial, middle, and final stages of the letter *kṣa*, which is the phoneme of reabsorption, [it includes] the letters *ka* and *ṣa*.

Together with the three [vowels] divided by the syllables *aḥ*, there are eleven; the sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*) is the Mother-phoneme (*mātṛkā*) situated at the end, while the sequence of consciousness (*saṃvitkrama*) is the state of the Goddesses of the channels (*vāhadevī*) being established in their own essential nature. || 6 ||
Now, in order to introduce the Sequence of the Nameless (Anākhyakrama), he says:
"Within the heart-lake of the petals, there is a perfectly circular segment with ten lines;
therein resides the primordial god, the fierce one consisting of thirteen and seventeen syllables who pervades the world. (7)
For each of the sequences beginning with emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), an internal period (*antardaśā*) is possible through other sequences;
thus, within the sequence of emanation, there is the inclusion of maintenance (*sthiti*), withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), and the unnameable (*anākhyā*).
The same applies to the sequences of maintenance and withdrawal. Now, how can there be an "unnameable" [period] for emanation, or an "unnameable" for maintenance?

And that which is called "the withdrawal" (saṃhāra) is distinct from the "nameless" (anākhya); thus, this has been rightly stated: if the one supreme reality, being inherently devoid of attributes (nirupādhi), enters into differentiation when qualified by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), then its division into creation, the nameless, and so forth has ensued, and that—
It has been asked: "Is even the Untouchable (*asparśa*) thus designated by association with the sequence of emanation and so forth? It is said: "In the root-lake" (*mūla*);

in the root-lake, which is the nature of the Inexplicable (*anākhyarūpa*), it manifests as four sections along with the sequence of emanation and so forth that is being projected from it. This [manifestation] is by its own nature as the Inexplicable, colored by the meaning of the sequence.

The primordial goddess, brilliantly shining in this world known as the aggregate of the lineage, blazes forth as the thirteenth [vowel] consisting of seventeen phonemes, like a fierce ray of light; this is the wheel of emanation (*sṛṣṭicakra*),
whose nature is emanation and which rests solely in emanation, and the wheel of maintenance (*sthiticakra*), whose nature is maintenance and which rests solely in maintenance.

The *saṃhāracakra* (wheel of withdrawal) has the form of withdrawal and rests solely in withdrawal; it is merely the rest in the essential nature of the three sequences, and not the internalization of the fourth sequence (*turyakrama*). In the *anākhyacakra* (wheel of the Inexplicable), however, even though emission contains the sequence, it rests solely in the emission that is beyond sequence (*anākhyaviśrānta*); and even though maintenance contains the sequence, [it likewise rests in the Inexplicable].

The state of persistence is the "Inexplicable Supreme" (*sthityanākhyaparā*), and dissolution, though containing within it a sequential process, culminates in the "Inexplicable Dissolution" (*saṃhārānākhyaparāyaṇa*).

These three stages of the Inexplicable (*anākhyabhūmi*) are characterized by limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*); they attain a state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) within the root-ground of the Inexplicable Abode (*anākhyadhāman*), which is free from all adjuncts (*nirupādhika*). This is the sequence of emanation and the rest.

This entire manifestation has been revealed for the sake of resting in the unnameable nature that constitutes the root; thus, this proliferation is subordinate to that. The supreme process of non-proliferation is to be contemplated, for even within the non-proliferated sequence of the Unnameable, there is a proliferation. (p. 120)
Arising from the Inexplicable, consisting of the Inexplicable, established in the Inexplicable, and resting in the Inexplicable— thus,

preceded by such differentiation, it is that which rests in non-differentiation; it is one alone, in the form of the manifestation of indivisible consciousness, consisting of the sequence of the Inexplicable, and composed of aesthetic integration (*sāmarasya*) through the dissolution of duality.
This is of great significance. Herein, the sequence of the abodes (*dhāmakrama*) is the very establishment of the primordial Goddess’s own nature;

the sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*) is the emergence of the resonance (*rāva*); and the sequence of consciousness (*saṃvitkrama*) is the subsiding of that resonance—this is the sequence of the Great Withdrawal (*mahāsaṃhārakrama*). || 7 ||
Now, he describes the rest of these very stages as they find repose in the successively higher state that is free from obscuration:
"When the breaths are calculated by fives, O Goddess, the sixty parts are experienced;
when the root of the lunar day (tithi) and so forth is rotated by five, it is seen as devoid of characteristics. (8)
The twelve vehicles (*vāha*), having sequentially attained the number sixty through the five leftward-moving goddesses (*vāmeśī*),
and being further multiplied by the four [movements] beginning with emission (*sṛṣṭi*), come to possess the number sixty-four; thus,
having transcended the sixty-fourth stage (*bhūmikā*), it takes the form of its conclusion.
The sixty-fifth great purpose desires the specific stage for the sake of the state of aesthetic integration (*sāmarasya*) as the place of rest for all; such is this Great Sequence (*mahākrama*). 8.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Mahānayaprakāśa composed by the venerable teacher Śitikaṇṭha. 10.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.

Having explained this very Great Sequence (mahākrama) by way of the sequence of consciousness (saṃvitkrama), he now describes it by way of the sequence of the abodes (dhāmakrama) as objects for individual worship.
I perceive this power called Nāda, which is fivefold in its radiance and auspicious;
I discern this innate nature, wherein dissolution and emergence occur spontaneously. || 1 ||
This very power called Anākhyā, having withdrawn its fourfold expansion, rests within the abode of consciousness itself; thus, although it has entered the sequence of consciousness,

because there is no separation between the sequence of consciousness and the sequence of the abode, it manifests once again through the sequence of the abode and, subsequently, through the sequence of manifestation.

It arose; for this is the nature of things regarding the existence of the supreme Brahman, which is without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*) and without abode (*nirdhāman*): that dissolution is followed by emergence, and emergence is followed by dissolution;
thus, dissolution and emergence occur only once, not by chance. || 1 ||
In order to experience this very [reality], he says:
"The supreme unmanifest, which is beyond all conceptualization, manifests as the world-phenomena; it is both with desire and without desire.
It reaches its own state, possessing tranquility; it shines forth as both the manifest and the unmanifest. (2)

The meaning of the *krama*, consisting of the entire manifold universe, was brought forth and directly realized by means of the first-syllable-portion (*ādyakṣarakalā*) arisen from the supreme ether; then, at the end, as it subsides into its own state, this *krama* has been rendered non-sequential (*akramīkṛta*), and once again it has been manifested in that same way through the sequence of manifestation (*bhāsākrama*).
Thus the summarized meaning [is concluded]. || 2 ||
He defines that sequence of sounds by the number of syllables:
"By the combination of the carriers of light as they move through the sun, three, four, four, and four; (p.
123) by the light crowded with the triple net of rays, eighteen, fourteen, and nine. (3)
For in this sequence of manifestation (*bhāsākrama*), four stages— known as the Total (*sakala*), the Total-and-Partless (*sakalaniṣkala*), the Partless (*aniṣkala*), and the Supreme (*parā*)—

illuminate the Sequence (*krama*) and the Great Sequence (*mahākrama*). Among these, in the Total Sequence (*sakalakrama*), there is a fixed number of twelve for the *cakriṇīs*, and within each *cakriṇī*-mantra, it is delimited by a number of eighteen.

There is a restriction regarding the phonemes (*varṇa-niyama*); and in the sequence of the manifest and unmanifest (*sakala-niṣkala-krama*), there is a sixfold restriction concerning the Goddesses of the Wheel (*cakriṇī-niyama*). In that [sixfold] sequence, four [mantras] consist of eighteen syllables like the manifest sequence, while two consist of fourteen syllables like the unmanifest sequence;

and in the unmanifest sequence, there are three Goddesses of the Wheel consisting of fourteen syllables; and in the supreme sequence, there is only one Kula-vidyā consisting of nine syllables—thus [it is].

There is a fixed number for the *cakriṇīs* and their respective mantras; consequently, the triad of abodes (*dhāmatrayī*) attains manifestation through the illumination of its own nature. Thus it is said that "the abode" (*dhāma*), because the solar [abodes] are twelve by nature, [taken] from among the sixteen lunar ones, ten remain.

Having been brought to a state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) within the self by means of the ten blazing *āgneya* channels, there remain six channels that are both with and without parts (*sakalaniṣkalā*).
Furthermore, there are three *āgneya* channels—namely *tāpanī*, *karālā*, and *lelihā*—which constitute the culmination and are extremely fierce, residing in the partless (*niṣkala*) state. Thus.
The three sequences are pervaded by the three abodes; and the Supreme Sequence—whose abode is beyond all abodes—is peaceful, proximate to Nirvāṇa, and is not touched by the abodes.
Thus, having caused the three abodes, which are filled with flames, to shine forth through individual immersion and having realized them directly...
It manifests with eighteen, fourteen, or nine syllables. || 3 ||
Now he describes the state of its purification: "The sixteen digits of the moon, enveloped by Agni and Soma, are here of the nature of the Bindu;
the twelve digits of the sun and the ten digits of fire—these five together, I purify. (4)
Below the Bindu, by means of the reflection of the Fire of Time (*kālāgni*),
and above the Kuṇḍalinī, by means of the lunar effusion, there is a constant state consisting of Fire and Moon;
through the merging of its ten and sixteen digits, it possesses twenty-six digits, as does the solar abode.
There are twelve *kalās* of the sun, sixteen of the moon, and ten of fire;

thus, the abode (*dhāman*) consisting of sixty-four *kalās* dissolves into the sixty-fifth, which is the abodeless (*nirdhāman*). This is the entry of the sequence of light, which consists of the abodes, into the state that is beyond all abodes. || 4 ||
He concludes this very point:

"The stainless mirror of the yoginī, which is the abode of the sequence of the letters, having made the pure syllables of the two feet of Praśānta-bhagavatī empty, she [the Yoginī] arises once again from that. (5)
That very consciousness, being of such a nature, attains tranquility in that state without ever fading. Why is this so? He says:

"of which," and so forth. It means that it is pacified in that abode consisting of absolute non-duality, wherein sequential and non-sequential natures, though distinct, arise. And of what nature is it? He says: "pure."
"In a stainless mirror, in a spotless looking-glass, [the reflection] is equal to that mirror which has come into the reflection"—
thus he states the illustrative example, beginning with "empty" and so forth, which constitutes a component of the mathematical process of both addition and subtraction;
for in calculation, the commencement is from zero, and there is a return to that very same point.
The Wheel of Speech. || 5 ||

Now he describes the ritual procedure of Samayeśvarī: "O Samayeśvara, through the division of the five groups of letters, one avoids the omission of rules; O fulfiller of desired objects, one performs the oblations with the full-offering. (6)

The occasion for the introduction of the *samaya-vidyā* is for the purpose of manifesting the unimpeded nature of the fruit that has been described regarding the expansion of the desired mantra; however, in other systems,
because of the state of equal primacy, the instruction on the *samaya-vidyā* is seen for each individual wheel (*cakra*).

And in this *Atinayasārasarvasva*, which concerns the meaning of the sequence (*krama*), since all sequences find their rest in that very final stage and that alone is primary, there is only one *samayavidyā*; and she is the fulfiller of the fruits described in various different sequences— thus, she is indeed the womb of the sequence (*kramagarbhā*).

By means of the differentiation of the various sequences of meanings up to the *ahaṃkāra*, through the division of the extent of the phonemes, and by preventing the loss of the specific fruits declared for the *kalpa*, it is "the accomplisher of the goal," like the *pūrṇāhuti*.
As the Mīmāṃsā text states: "Just as one attains all desires through the *pūrṇāhuti*."

Just as the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) bestows its fruit for the production of a new result from that which was previously prepared for the purpose of a sacrifice, so too does this [final initiation].
He says that very thing:
"At the time of emanation, in the weapon-mantra, the fierce one—thus indeed, may the lotus-born one consume [it].
The five-fold abode consisting of the state of burning, O goddess, in the center of the navel... || 7 ||
O Gāsukari, O Bindivāteu, O Satikakhahasubhaṅkara, O Śiva-Śiva!
O Leader of all Siddhis, O Eternal Śiva who abides in the convention of external manifestation! 8.
The cow-eater (*gāsukarī*) should be contemplated as the *bindu*.
(The Tilaka:
This very one is the Mistress of the Timeless Convention (*anākhyasamayeśvarī*), the Blessed One of the Convention (*samayā bhagavatī*), by means of the first Great Weapon (*mahāstra*).

With two phonemes, he consumes the lotus-born [Brahmā] from the *kanda*; he removes this lotus-born one's state of being an obstacle to the attainment of his own true nature by the practitioners (*upāsakas*). Likewise, with the other fifteen phonemes, through the *sthiti-anākhyā-samaya*, [he consumes] Padmanābha from the location of the navel.
He makes Viṣṇu subtle— meaning he effects the absence of any obstruction even in his own central channel (*madhyama-nāḍī*) within the apertures; with sixty-nine phonemes,
from the center of the Mistress of the Time of Reabsorption (*saṃhārānākhyasamayeśvarī*), he strikes down Rudra from the vicinity of the heart, just like that.

That is to say, she acts without obstruction. She herself, as the pure Mistress of the Unnamed Time (*anākhyasamayeśvarī*), loosens the Lord from his face and other [limbs] by means of two syllables. And becoming the Mistress of the Radiant Time (*bhāsāsamayeśvarī*), she removes Sadāśiva from the Bindu by means of the twelve subsequent syllables; thus, she consists of one hundred syllables.
Even when divided, she remains undivided; having meditated upon all perfections and supernatural powers (*sarvasiddhi-ṛddhi*), she becomes the bestower of good fortune.
Thus it is auspicious, most auspicious—how wonderful! This concludes the "Devouring of the Five Causes" (*kāraṇapañcakagrāsa*) of the *Samayavidyā*. 7–8.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the Mahānayaprakāśa composed by the venerable teacher Śitikaṇṭha. 11.
Now begins the twelfth [chapter], the Arising.
One should recognize this as that which is eternal, universal, and perfectly manifest; thus he says:
"If the intellect is not cultivated through discernment, one would perceive the Supreme Consciousness as if it were being struck by an axe."
Know that the world is composed of the reflections of sense-objects; O Goddess, come to me and worship me. || 1 ||
By this division of the wheels and the Mistress of the Wheels, which contains within it the sequence of emanation and so forth,
that which is in every form is in reality shown to be nothing but the touch of consciousness; therein, one should consider that the mere touch of consciousness alone is the essence.
Is it not observed that there is an immersion into the various levels (*bhūmikā*) of consciousness with respect to their respective objects? To address this, he says "object" (*viṣaya*):

the object exists as being entered by consciousness merely by its shadow; that too must be contemplated as having consciousness as its ultimate reality (*cit-paramārtha*). How so? He says "the Goddess" (*devī*): the meaning is, having effected an immersion into the body of the Goddess.
For all these worldly activities are both differentiated and non-differentiated— composed and divided; yet,
because external objects lack their own essential nature through their own power (due to their being manifest as distinct forms),
they do not exist [as independent entities], or if they did exist, there would be a mutual contradiction of the intrinsic natures of things, since the ultimate reality is consciousness alone.

Through connection with consciousness, through immersion in consciousness, through consciousness being the ultimate reality, and through resting in consciousness, these things attain their foundation; one must settle in the mind that there exists no other self-originated nature of entities whatsoever. || 1 ||

Regarding this, he states the reasoning for proceeding further with the verse: "The supreme union is that which, having been thoroughly cleansed, brings about the state of the void; the supreme goal is like a python that has consumed the food of worldly existence. (p. 131)

The heart (*hṛdaya*) is said to be the essential core of the true nature (*satattva-sāra*) of things in their individual, specific forms; and that, ultimately, resolves into nothing other than imperishable pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Whatever object is sought for union with the Self, in its fusion with the Heart as described, there occurs a state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) with one's own Self.

It should be remembered— the meaning is that the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the object of knowledge (*vedya*) is to be characterized precisely as the true essence of the ultimate reality of the knower (*vedaka*). However, once that state has been assimilated into one's own being (*ātmasātkriyamāṇa*),
it is not appropriate to have a repeated fixation (*abhiniveśa*) characterized by a longing for it, through the equilibrium of existence and non-existence (*bhāvābhāvasāmarasya*).

For that which is called the "Ajagara-vow" (the python's vow) is the perfected nature of the subject (*pramātṛdharma*), and it alone is to be embraced with every effort as the ultimate reality by those of keen intellect. || 2 ||

Surely, those who fear worldly existence must, for the sake of removing that fear, request some means of dramatic representation (abhinaya) originating from a lineage, through the process of worship directed toward the mouth of a guru; in that regard, what occasion is there for discourses on consciousness? For you—
One who bathes with sesame, rubs himself with sesame, performs fire-oblations with sesame, offers water with sesame,
eats sesame, and gives away sesame— the one who practices these six ways with sesame does not perish.

Having thus [stated that], one might raise the doubt: "Since pure consciousness alone has been made the instrument throughout all the procedures by means of total expenditure [of its own nature], how does it come to rest?
Anticipating this, he says:
In the entry of the wheel, the body of time consists of pure consciousness;
it is to be worshipped in the entry of the state of the Ṛṣis, within the constant meditative absorption of the body. || 3 ||

It has been stated that one should bring to completion, in a single, vast body of Kālī, that very conduct of the wheels and their sovereign goddesses which was received from the mouth of the Guru— conduct that remains unbroken and is established for worship through repeated effort; thus, by means of "parts" (*bhāgaiḥ*), that [conduct] is [achieved] through the divisions of parts and the entry into each respective wheel.

Worship, as previously described, should be cultivated through the penetration of the heart-lotus and through constant meditative absorption within the body that consists of pure consciousness (cinmaya) which is free from limiting adjuncts (nirupādhi), by way of its being the innermost self; thus, nothing has been neglected. || 3 ||
And this very reality of the ultimate goal, handed down through tradition, belongs to the *pīṭhacarīs* in all the sacred seats (*pīṭhas*). Thus he says:
"The enjoyment of existence is to be made an object of consciousness; this is the beloved place of the *khecarīs*."
O Bhairava, you desire to perform the embrace of the Ālī; may there be the essence of that union. || 4 ||

When the doubt arises as to what the enjoyment (*bhoga*) of an object (*bhāva*) is, it is simply the act of making it an object of consciousness (*cid-viṣayīkaraṇa-mātra*) that constitutes the purpose of enjoyment according to traditional transmission; that alone is the beloved abode of the *khecarīs*, the goddesses of the channels (*vāhadevī*).
And those channel-goddesses, having tasted each respective [object] of the senses...

They offer themselves as the Bhairava of consciousness; finally, by surrendering their very selves, they abandon [the object] and find rest within it—thus, the enjoyment of the object is the locus of culmination. || 4 ||
Considering this alone to be most worthy of aspiration, he said:
"Delighted by the words of the guru, one should dwell in solitude; one should practice yoga and conquer the senses.
One should dwell with a heart free from all dualities, and avoid all forms of indulgence. (5)
Thus, being ever-joyful, having rested the lineage of the supreme Guru within his heart,
considering rest to be in the Akrama preceded by the touch of the Krama,
and having assimilated every state of being into himself, he abandons attachment to external objects— everything.
Lead him away. || 5 ||
Considering this alone to be worthy of aspiration, he said:

"In constant meditative absorption, possessing the power of *ḍala*, one is exalted in the practice and non-practice; abiding in both the mundane and supramundane, this is the task to be undertaken, established in the ultimate method. (6)

May those who have reached the culmination of the method, possessing supreme accomplishment through constant attentiveness practiced with abundance, and abiding on both the mundane and supramundane paths, thus partake in the meaning of the stages in every aspect. (6)
And this has been forgotten by everyone; thus he says:

"By whom the great path from the mouth of the Guru was heard—by that very [means], all those who have fallen into the cycle of existence have crossed over the ocean of the world, which consists of the eightfold collection of beings, and have become great persons. (7)

In the fourteen worlds, this eternal light of consciousness—known by the great name *Mahārtha* and synonymous with one's own true nature (*svarūpa*)—remains unobstructed and perfectly manifest, even amidst the fourteenfold creation of beings.
Yet, due to the immersion in objective existence (*bhāvāveśa*), it has receded from the path of memory for all; it remains as if lost, while they [the beings] remain [caught in their delusion].
The great people— those for whom the Guru’s mouth has thus become manifest,

and by whom the nature of the seven Great Meanings has been thoroughly cultivated— he who awakens the rays of touch residing in all the pores of the skin, he is this one who has become of a single flavor in the central abode, the object of the nine wheels.

The tradition is manifested through mutual vitalization; likewise, in the *pīṭhacakra*, there is a threefold pervasion: the pervasion of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the pervasion of the gross elements (*bhūta*), and the pervasion of the five currents (*pañcavāha*). Within the five currents, along with the repose in the emanation and other stages of the Great Sequence (*mahākrama*), there is also the pervasion of the mudrās such as Karaṅkiṇī.
And the pervasion of the fivefold deities through the sequence of the *vṛnda*— thus the state of pervasion is indeed threefold;
[it occurs] through the forms of light, bliss, and the body (the sun,
moon, and fire), and through mind, intellect, and ego, and through the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and through the triad of emanation and so forth— it is indeed threefold.
The state of pervasion (*vyāptisthiti*) consists of the circle of the assembly (*vṛndacakra*), wherein there are as many deities as there are sixty-four seats (*pīṭha*).

Their sixty-four accomplishments (*siddhi*) take the form of the planes of consciousness (*saṃvidbhūmikā*), because through the pervasion of the five currents (*pañcavāha*), each of the twelve rays becomes sixty, and there are four root goddesses (*mūladevī*). Thus it is said.

There are sixty-four levels of consciousness (*cidbhūmikā*); this is the pervasion of the levels of consciousness. Likewise, there are thirty-eight *kalās* and twenty-six *baindavyas*; thus, there is the pervasion of the *dhāma-kalās* by means of these sixty-four. [This is further characterized] by the fifteen vowels: the short, long, and prolated.

The sequence of the sixty-four phonemes (*varṇakrama*) consists of the eight diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*), the four restraints (*yama*), and likewise the consonants (*vyañjana*) combined together; thus, it is ninefold— namely, by means of the five wheels beginning with the Five Streams (*pañcavāha*) as taught by the Goddess Makāra,
along with the four Great Sequences (*mahākrama*), and likewise by means of the four Light-Sequences (*bhāsākrama*).

"By means of the fivefold division of the Mistress of the Rule (Samayeśvarī), and thus by nine [divisions]— the state of the Rule (samayasthiti) is thus encapsulated within all [these divisions], like the fluid within a peacock's egg;
and there is a mutual [interrelation] among the divisions of the Mahākrama, the Bhāsākrama, and the Samayeśvarī."

In every way there is non-differentiation—thus, this entire essence of consciousness, both supreme and subordinate, having become of a single flavor, attains a state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) within the most transcendent abode of consciousness; such is the summarized meaning. || 7 ||
Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Mahānayaprakāśa* composed by the venerable teacher Śitikaṇṭha. 12.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter on arising.
Then, having selected a certain procedure, he says: "Whatever has been heard from the mouth of the Guru bears fruit; how could there be dispute regarding worship or transition?"
At one time, there was a single lamp-offering for the purpose of worshipping Coda. || 1 ||
Established in the supreme flood of emanation, in the divine flood, joined with the flood of the Saṃhitā, and in the flood of the Siddhas; (p.
138) the human flood does not describe enjoyment; the five floods are the light of the seats and the samaya. || 2 ||

If the face of the Guru has appeared before you without dispute, up until the attainment of the fruit, through the teachings on transference (*saṃkramaṇa*) and worship performed at a single time, then all three [empowerments] are possible, being established solely in the mouth of the Guru. That being so, when he is pleased:
Regarding the doubt as to whether all three [initiations] bear fruit at once or sequentially, this is the certainty:

after the transmission from the Guru, at the very beginning of the instruction, the teaching on worship must be completed within four days; this rule is not to be transgressed, and in this regard, such is our tradition from the mouth of the Guru.
First, preceded by the worship of the *pīṭhacakra*, there is the lineage of the Guru known as *paraugha*, the wheel of emanation (*sṛṣṭicakra*), and the sequence of manifestation (*bhāsākrama*);

therein, Samayeśvarī is to be worshipped—this constitutes one daily ritual sequence. By the second [sequence], likewise preceded by the worship of the *pīṭhacakra*, there is the lineage of the Guru known as *divyaugha* and the sequence of maintenance (*sthitikrama*).

As previously stated, the sacrifice consists of exactly five types, together with Bhāsā and Samayeśvarī. On the third day, at the *pīṭhacakra*, these five are to be worshipped: the Great Flood (*mahaugha*), the lineage of Gurus (*gurukrama*), the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), and the pair Bhāsā and Samayeśvarī. And on the fourth [day], the *pīṭhacara*.

The lineage of the Siddhas, the lineage of the Mānavas, the lineage of the Śiṣyas, the Anākhyakrama, the Bhāsākrama, and Samayeśvarī—these five alone are to be worshipped; this is the remainder [of the instruction]. || 1 || 2 ||
Now he states the procedure for the *arghapātra* (the vessel of honor): "The five-fold sequence of the Guru’s convention is placed in the *cupāva*; the *trepāva* is the foremost.
The *bindu* at the mouth of the goat (*ajamukha*) is the reversal of the *jañī*; that which is called *akumuṇḍa* is the excellence of the *aścanasa*. (3)
One should worship the lineages of the gurus and the Mistress of the Samaya in a vessel placed upon a four-legged seat;
likewise, in a vessel placed upon a three-legged seat, well-perfumed, purified by the ritual consecration of the vessel,
filled with the *argha* offering containing the supreme liquor obtained from the two jewels, and reflecting one's own face.

One should worship at the conclusion of the fourfold sequence; then, one should pour the remnant of the yellow [liquid] from the former vessel, turned face down, into the space of the skull (muṇḍavyoman), and likewise join the latter vessel, containing the arghya and turned face down, to the place of worship. || 3 ||
He states the sequence of the lamps (*dīpakrama*) by means of a pair of verses:

"The lineage of the supreme divine great-siddhas (*mahāsiddhaugha*), the human lineage (*mānavaugha*), and the lineage of the gurus (*gurukrama*)—these five lineages follow the five stages (*krama*) in their application (*upayoga*), together with the enjoyment (*bhoga*) of the wheel of seats (*pīṭhacakra*) and the commitments (*samaya*). (4)
O thief, O thief! The five days of the sun [are spent] in the whirling of the wheel of desire; the messenger of death reveals himself.
Or else, for the sake of the lamp of life, find a moment’s respite even for a single day.
(A pair of verses:

"The sacrifice for the sake of the sequence (*kramārthayāga*) is to be completed with the *caru* offering made manifest over five days, together with one female messenger (*dūtī*), by one who abides by the rule (*samayastha*); such is the teaching from the mouth of our Guru. How so? He says: "Those who... (*ye pare...*).
Through the unification of the flood of human beings and the flood of disciples, there are five lineages of gurus;

by following each of these lineages in succession—one lineage per day—five lineages are to be worshipped over five days. At the beginning and at the end of each, in every instance, [the worship is performed] with the Pīṭha, the Cakra, the Samaya, and the Īśvarī.

There are four places of worship each day— this is the rule for the pair— and in this way, the Mistress of the Four Wheels (Catuścakreśvarī) becomes worshipped. Alternatively, on a single day, when the requisite collection of ritual materials has been obtained, [one may worship] by means of the assembly consisting of thirteen members.
The concluding rite (pāraṇīya) is to be performed as described in the *Pūjātilaka*; thus, this ritual procedure is complete. || 4 || 5 ||
The majesty of the Buddhas is peerless; it is established as a single, solid mass. This great essence is secret and sublime, revealed only to those noble people who possess pure hearts. 6.

O virtuous people, may that secret place called the Great Tradition (*mahāmnāya*), which is fortified by four powers—the physical (*ādhibhautika*), the divine (*adhidaivika*), the spiritual (*adhyātmika*), and the all-pervasive (*sarvātmika*)—shine forth in the minds of you who are possessed of supreme conduct. And of what nature is it? To this he says:
It has attained a state of single compactness, experienced and realized by the ancient perfected ones who were fully endowed with the tradition; as it was stated (p.
142), this occurred in accordance with the fourfold power, and furthermore, it was rendered free from obstacles through the fourfold rite of offering (*balikarman*).
The attainment of the fruit of supreme bliss has been completed. || 6 ||
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Mahānayaprakāśa* composed by the venerable teacher Śitikaṇṭha. 13.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter, "The Arising.
May the Lord, out of his grace, protect this work here; the birth of the Blue-Necked One has reached its fulfillment.
By him, through the grace of the Great Person (Mahājana), may the supreme goal of the great sages be attained. 1.
Having attained such a sequence through the grace of the Lord, my birth as Śitikaṇṭha has reached fulfillment;
by me, who have thus accomplished my purpose, even the great people have been reminded of the Great Purpose and the Ultimate Reality. May there be auspiciousness! || 1 ||

Through eighteen divisions, it reached its full development as the wheel of nine in the center, pervading the preceding and following [stages]. That supreme, pure-radiant wheel, which is called the "Meditation" (*dhyāna*) among the sequences,
shines forth from this [source] as the various parts of that non-duality which is supremely intent on revealing the Great Purpose (*mahārtha*).
May both we and you enter into that state which is accumulated, stainless, indivisible, and of a single nature.

May those various manifestations enter into and pervade both us—our own—and you—yourselves—their activity being one whose unity is accumulated, stainless, and unbroken; that is, it has reached full growth (*upacitā*), attained expansion;
it is stainless (*vimalā*), untouched by the turbidity of duality; and it is unbroken (*akhaṇḍitā*), all-pervasive. Which [activity]? That which...
"May they enter into that state through the mode of identity"—the meaning is "may they plunge into it," "may they bestow it," or "may they penetrate it.
Of what nature are they? They shine forth from this supreme non-duality (*paramādvaita*) which is the manifestation of the Great Meaning (*mahārtha*);
that is, the manifestation of the Great Meaning is "mahārthaprakaṭana," and by means of that manifestation of the Great Meaning, there is supreme non-duality.

The supreme non-duality (*paramādvaita*) is the manifestation of the Great Purpose (*mahārtha*); therefore, "those who shine through delusion" means that all things, while appearing as such, are in fact manifest as the Great Purpose. As was stated previously:
"That which is like the ocean of white milk, [is] the dance of consciousness (*citanyānṛtta*) of that very one."

Thus, from what [reason] is this so? He says: "Because this Wheel of the Ineffable (anākhyacakra) has undergone transformation through eighteen terminal divisions. Those which have eighteen at their end are "eighteen-terminal" (aṣṭādaśānta); by means of those eighteen-terminals. And these are the "divisions of parts" (aṃśabheda)—the divisions of the parts.
The six [streams] are the Pīṭhacakra, Paraugha, Divyaugha, Mahaugha, Siddhaugha, and Mānavaugha;

and the three wheels of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal—thus the previous group of nine. Likewise, Samayeśvarī and the rest are fivefold, consisting of the forms: Sakala, Asakala, Niṣkala, and Pararūpa.

The fourfold sequence of speech has undergone transformation through eighteen variations ending with the final limit. Furthermore, of what nature is it? He says: "Pervasive," meaning all-encompassing. In the middle of what? He says:
"Of the nine and the nine"—that is, of those which are prior and posterior; they are both the nine that were before and the nine that are after.

"Of those nine, of the nine preceding and succeeding ones"—that is, of the sequences such as creation and so forth—He is the most excellent (*vara*), the supreme, the presiding overlord of all. "Vimalā" means whose splendor (*ruci*)—that is, light—is stainless, free from the turbidity of objects; thus it is. This is a benedictory statement.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Mahānayaprakāśa composed by the illustrious Śitikaṇṭhācārya, the most eminent teacher of the Great Māheśvara tradition. || 14 ||
And this *Mahānayaprakāśa* is completed. (p.145) When the assembly of texts and learned scholars among those possessing true knowledge had fallen into decline due to the course of time...
For the sake of his livelihood, he was devoted solely to the desire to uphold the various true dharmas, endowed with the vigor of right discernment. || 1 ||
Having deliberated with his principal ministers who were devoted to righteousness, the illustrious sovereign of Kaśmīra established [this work],
which is pregnant with spiritual knowledge and realized wisdom.
That which is the principal office for the extraction of texts. || 2 ||
May this [work], being refined by the virtuous who enter upon the holy life (*ājīva*), who rely on Mukunda as their presiding lord, and who are devoted to Rāma—
being perfected, purified, and explained— attain completion.
This completed work is for the welfare of virtuous people. || 3 ||
(Tilaka) May this [offering] become an auspicious dedication to one's own Self as Śiva.
